pillars.engagement_stem: You are more likely to contribute your time, effort and identity into a group

GrpProsp.name: Group Prospects
GrpProsp.description: How far you feel the group, as it now stands, can pull off the venture it has taken on and not yet finished: a game, project, season or campaign. It is confidence in the capability the venture will run on, not luck, not your own prospects (Payoff), not whether each will do their part (Dependability) and not a general sense that the group is strong. The culture's face sets where that capability is looked for.
GrpProsp.footnote: A group with goals is formally defined as a team, but the term group is preferred as it removes the implication of a wider organisation and hierarchy.

anchors.10: You feel sure the group, as it stands, can pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks well within its reach.
anchors.1: You feel sure the group, as it stands, cannot pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks beyond it.

GrpProsp.effect_on_other_pillars: GrpProsp's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute. In other words, the goal still remains to be achieved.
GrpProsp.engagement: That is likely to succeed in goals that you believe are worth pursing, or you would not have joined the group in the first place, and that has agreed goals, or otherwise random changes to the group's direction will move outside the model's ability to predict.
GrpProsp.out_of_scope: Random changes to the group's direction without agreed goals.

pre_language.core: A felt sense, before any words, that this band can bring off what it is setting out to do: the chimpanzee weighing the hunting party and feeling the colobus within reach when enough able hunters are present, and out of reach when they are not. Intimates read it from her bearing as the venture starts: settled and forward-leaning, in step with the others, or hesitant and watchful, eyes on the others rather than the task.

GrpProsp.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
GrpProsp.gloss: Felt confidence the group can pull this off

excluded: Generalised group potency: 'overarching group efficiency' and the generic ability to coordinate on any venture ('hunting ANY animal').
Process efficacy: confidence in the group's coordination, communication and cooperation as such ('ability to coordinate effectively').
Outcome forecast ('will achieve'), including fortune: a probability that the goal comes about, from whatever cause.
The rule that achieved goals drop out and 'may not continue to influence your engagement'.
Personal objectives within the group.

era.why: Chimpanzees weigh their party's strength before joining an intergroup contest (Wilson, Hauser and Wrangham 2001), and early humans' joint foraging needed a felt sense that the group could bring the hunt off; no talk is needed for that confidence.

E.label: Capability spread across the members
E.description: How far you feel the group, as it now stands, can pull off the venture it has agreed to take on and not yet finished. It is confidence in the group's capability for that venture, spread across its members, their skill included, and including whoever the band looks to for this venture for the day, so long as they lead by being followed and not by command. It is not luck, not your own prospects (Payoff), not whether each will do their part (Dependability), and not a general sense that the group is strong.

anchors.10: You feel sure the group, as it stands, can pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks well within its reach.
anchors.1: You feel sure the group, as it stands, cannot pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks beyond it.

E.subtitle: Group's capability to finish its venture
E.summary: Team Confidence, egalitarian face, is how far you feel the group as it now stands can pull off the venture it has agreed to take on and not yet finished. It counts capability spread across the members, skill included, and whoever the band looks to for the day, if they lead by being followed. It is not luck, Payoff, Dependability or general group strength.
E.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

H.label: Confidence in those who steer
H.description: How far you feel those at the top of the order, yourself included if you are there, can steer the group through the venture it has taken on and not yet finished: read the ground, choose the course, set each member to the part that suits them and right the course when it goes wrong. It reads their competence to direct this venture only. It is not whether they push you about or take more than their due (Parity), not the deference you draw for what you bring (Esteem), not your rung in the order (Rank), not what staying will bring you (Payoff), and not whether those below will carry their parts (Dependability). A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low; a hard one who knows the way rates high.

anchors.10: You feel sure those at the top know the way through what the group has taken on; you follow their lead without second-guessing it, and if you are among them you feel the course is in safe hands.
anchors.1: You feel sure those at the top cannot steer the group through what it has taken on; each call they make looks like the wrong one, and if you are among them you feel the course slipping out of your hands.

pre_language.core: A felt sense, before any words, that the ones in front know where to take the band: the troop's readiness to rise and follow when the lead animal moves off, as subordinate chacma baboons follow the dominant male's foraging moves even at a cost to themselves (King et al. 2008), against hanging back, lagging or drifting off when the lead's moves have come to nothing. Read with care: in King's troops the closest followers were the leader's grooming partners, so following rests on ties as well as on any reading of where he leads; and in olive baboons movement is settled among many initiators and the dominant is not simply followed (Strandburg-Peshkin et al. 2015), so the form belongs to despotic orders. Intimates read it from how she meets a call from the top: moving with it at once, eyes on the task, or a pause, a glance at the others and a slow, half-hearted start; and, if she is at the front herself, from a sure, unhurried move off against a false start and a look back.

H.subtitle: Confidence the leaders can steer
H.summary: Team Confidence, hierarchical face, is how far you feel those at the top, you included if you are there, can steer the group through its unfinished venture: reading the ground, choosing the course, placing members in suitable parts and righting mistakes. It rates their competence only. It is not Parity, Esteem, Rank, Payoff or Dependability. A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low.
H.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

sources.source: Dirks, K. T. (2000). Trust in leadership and team performance: Evidence from NCAA basketball. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(6), 1004-1012.
sources.claim: In men's college basketball teams, players' trust in the coach both resulted from and predicted team performance. Grounds the hierarchical face as a reading of the top that bears on the venture; the trust measure is broader than competence, so only its competence part is taken.
sources.verified: yes, at abstract level; sample details not checked against full text

sources.source: Dirks, K. T., and Ferrin, D. L. (2002). Trust in leadership: Meta-analytic findings and implications for research and practice. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(4), 611-628.
sources.claim: Meta-analysis (k = 106) of trust in leadership with outcomes, antecedents and correlates; direct leaders are a particularly important referent; links with attitudes such as commitment are stronger than with performance (reported in the authors' earlier conference version). Trust there mixes competence with good faith, so the face takes it as light support and leaves good faith to Levelling and Reciprocity.
sources.verified: partly; abstract and conference summary seen, correlation tables not seen

sources.source: Chen, G., and Bliese, P. D. (2002). The role of different levels of leadership in predicting self- and collective efficacy: Evidence for discontinuity. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(3), 549-556.
sources.claim: In 2,585 soldiers from 86 combat units, leadership climate at the higher organisational level was the strongest predictor of collective efficacy. Grounds placing a ranked group's confidence in its capability on how its upper leadership is read.

sources.source: Meindl, J. R., Ehrlich, S. B., and Dukerich, J. M. (1985). The romance of leadership. Administrative Science Quarterly, 30(1), 78-102.
sources.claim: People over-attribute organisational outcomes to leadership, more so the more extreme the outcome. Grounds reading the venture's fortunes through those at the top, and warns that the face is inflated or sunk by results after the fact.
sources.verified: partly; bibliographic record and secondary summaries seen, abstract not seen

sources.source: Fiske, A. P. (1992). The four elementary forms of sociality: Framework for a unified theory of social relations. Psychological Review, 99(4), 689-723.
sources.claim: Authority ranking is one of four elementary relational models: people are ordered linearly, those above hold authority and privilege, and those below are owed guidance and protection. Grounds the hierarchical face's location of steering in those at the top.
sources.verified: partly; the four models and linear ordering confirmed, the guidance-and-protection detail from secondary summaries only

sources.source: King, A. J., Douglas, C. M. S., Huchard, E., Isaac, N. J. B., and Cowlishaw, G. (2008). Dominance and affiliation mediate despotism in a social primate. Current Biology, 18(23), 1833-1838.
sources.claim: Chacma baboon group foraging decisions were led by the dominant male, who gained most from them; subordinates followed despite consensus costs, and his closest grooming partners followed most closely. Pre-language form of the hierarchical face.

sources.source: Strandburg-Peshkin, A., Farine, D. R., Couzin, I. D., and Crofoot, M. C. (2015). Shared decision-making drives collective movement in wild baboons. Science, 348(6241), 1358-1361.
sources.claim: In GPS-tracked wild olive baboons, movement direction was settled among multiple initiators and dominant individuals were not simply followed. Bounds the pre-language form to despotic orders.

sources.source: Kruglanski, A. W., and Webster, D. M. (1991). Group members' reactions to opinion deviates and conformists at varying degrees of proximity to decision deadline and of environmental noise. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 61(2), 212-225.
sources.claim: In freely interacting groups, a deviate was rejected more when dissent came close to the group's decision deadline, attributed to heightened need for collective closure. Supports the retained mechanism of X:GrpProsp->NormExp.
sources.verified: yes for the first experiment, at abstract level; the other three experiments not checked

It is not their good faith or whether they push you about (Levelling), not the deference you draw for what you bring (Prestige), not your rung in the order (Status), not what staying will bring you (OwnProsp), and not whether those below will carry their parts (OutResp). edits.why: Hierarchical face only. Its clause 'not their good faith or whether they push you about (Levelling)' sends leaders' good faith to Levelling, which claims only force or fear and taking more than one's due and makes it stick. Good intent as such belongs to no perception, and the face's own closing line already rules it out ('A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low'). The fix points the Levelling clause at Levelling's actual ground and leaves good faith excluded by that closing line. The general definition, the egalitarian face and all anchors agree with OwnProsp, OutResp, Status, Prestige and Levelling boundary clauses and fit the collective-efficacy literature (Bandura 1997) and, for the hierarchical face, work tying confidence in the venture to confidence in its leaders (e.g. leader efficacy, Hannah et al. 2008; unchecked here). No change there.

edits.why: The boundary clauses agree with the other perceptions. OutResp's 'reliability, not skill (GrpProsp)' matches the E face's 'their skill included'. The H face's exclusions of Levelling, Prestige, Status, OwnProsp and OutResp match how those perceptions describe themselves, and nothing is left unclaimed or claimed twice. The literature fit is close: the E face is collective efficacy (Bandura 1997; Zaccaro et al. 1995) and the H face is confidence in a leader's competence, as distinct from benevolence (Dirks & Ferrin 2002). The brief asks for a short, general definition with no face text in it, and Reciprocity and Belonging already follow that pattern. Smallest fix: cut the face content from that sentence. The faces and anchors stay as they are.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'the chimpanzee weighing the hunting party and feeling the colobus within reach when enough able hunters are present, and out of reach when they are not'
problems.detail: No cited or sorted source covers chimpanzee colobus hunting or party size in hunts. Melis et al. 2006 is a captive rope-pulling task; Wilson et al. 2001 is intergroup contests. The hunting literature (for example Boesch 1994) may back it but is neither cited nor checked. Rest the image on the checked numerical-assessment and partner-choice findings instead.

problems.where: faces.H.pre_language.core: 'in King's troops the closest followers were the leader's grooming partners'
problems.detail: The checker found that following depended on social bonds or affiliation with the dominant male, not grooming partners by name. Say social bonds.

problems.where: faces.H.pre_language.core: 'so the form belongs to despotic orders'
problems.detail: Neither baboon paper sets that bound (checker: not in source for Strandburg-Peshkin et al. 2015). Two troops of two species show that single-leader following is one primate pattern among others. Restricting the form to ranked orders is a modelling choice and should say so.

logic_status.common_sense: The exclusions (not luck, not Payoff, not Dependability, not general group strength) and 'yourself included if you are there' are definitional boundaries, safe because they only partition the model's own perceptions. The intimate signs (forward-leaning and in step against hesitant and watchful; moving at once against a pause and a glance) are ordinary observation of confidence. 'A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low; a hard one who knows the way rates high' follows from defining the H face as competence only. The H face's location of confidence in the top rests on Dirks 2000 (supports) and Chen and Bliese 2002 (supports), with Meindl et al. 1985 (partly) as the caution; the E face's capability spread across members rests on Melis et al. 2006 (supports) and leaders who lead by being followed on von Rueden et al. 2014 (supports).

OwnProsp.name: Own Prospects
OwnProsp.description: How likely you feel it is that staying in this group will get you what you yourself are after from it: the place, play, pay, skill, advancement or mate you joined for. It is a forecast of what the group will deliver to you, not your own ability, not your present rung in the order (Rank), not the group's own venture (Team Confidence), not whether help you give comes back (Reciprocity), and not a tally of what it has given so far, which only feeds it.

anchors.10: You are sure that staying will bring you what you came for; the group's dealings with you keep opening the way to it.
anchors.1: You are sure that staying will bring you nothing you came for; whatever you do here, the way to it stays shut.

OwnProsp.effect_on_other_pillars: You respond to your current assessment of goal achievement likelihood.
OwnProsp.engagement: Where you feel that you are likely to achieve your personal goals, whether or not they are part of the group goals (Team Confidence) or indeed, conflict with them. Presumably if personal and group goals are in conflict, you would prefer to have low levels of Team Confidence however such a condition is out of scope for the model as it indicates deception and potentially sabotage, which is a cognitive rather than an unconscious drive (as the Pillars are contended to be).
OwnProsp.out_of_scope: Personal goals deliberately in conflict with group goals (deception, sabotage).

pre_language.core: The felt yield of staying with this band for her: whether being here keeps bringing her food, a mate, a place or a skill, or keeps bringing her nothing. Its animal form is the forager's reading that a patch is still worth working, and the primate's reading that staying in this troop will or will not yield what staying costs. Intimates read it from whether she settles in and works at her own aims here, or drifts to the edge, looks outward and leaves.

OwnProsp.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
OwnProsp.gloss: Will staying here get me what I want?

excluded: Own ability: self-efficacy or perceived competence, the 'can I do it' reading.
Satisfaction with what the group has delivered so far.
Hope as an emotion, and hope as agency plus pathways thinking.
Positive fantasies: vivid imagining of the desired outcome.
Comparison with outside alternatives: what she could get elsewhere.
Past achievement as evidence: achieved goals counting toward prospects.
Non-monotonic striving: strongest effort at intermediate likelihood.
Disengagement and re-engagement from unattainable goals.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'Its animal form is the forager's reading that a patch is still worth working, and the primate's reading that staying in this troop will or will not yield what staying costs.'
problems.detail: Two empirical claims about animal decision-making (patch-leaving, as in the marginal value theorem; primate dispersal decisions) with no cited or checked source. Calling them 'its animal form' asserts homology on top. Drop the sentence, or cite and check (for example Charnov 1976 and a primate dispersal study) and present them as analogues.

logic_status.common_sense: The whole definition rests on common sense: no source is cited, and the one sorted theory (Wageman 1995) concerns reward interdependence and effort, not this reading. Defining Payoff as a felt forecast of what staying will bring you, with boundaries against Rank, Team Confidence, Reciprocity and a running tally, is a definitional partition and safe. The intimate signs (settling in and working at one's own aims against drifting to the edge, looking outward and leaving) are ordinary observation of whether someone expects a place to pay off.

Status.name: Status
Status.description: Your felt rung in the group's settled order of precedence: how far you go first, take the first turn and the first share as a matter of course, and how far you go after others and take what is left. All recognise the order, so it is not fought out each time. The precedence attaches to your place, however you came by it: an office, seniority, the backing of kin or allies, an old contest no one reopens, or credit for what you bring that has settled, over time, into a place others take for granted. It is distinct from the live deference you draw for what you bring now (Esteem), and it is not held in place by present fear (Parity).

anchors.10: You go first as a matter of course: the first turn, the first share and the best seat are yours without a word said, and no one in the group stands above you.
anchors.1: You go last as a matter of course: you wait your turn and take your share and seat after everyone else, without a word said, and no one in the group stands below you.

Status.effect_on_other_pillars: Your perception of your status can change due to slight changes to a formal remit, or the willingness people are to be compelled. If they do not respect your authority, you would feel lower status, and influence your behaviour.
Status.engagement: Where you feel that you possess formal power within a group, enabling you to utilise the group to achieve your own vision, which aligns the group with your identity. This is why new leaders often revoke measures taken by the preceding.

pre_language.core: Her felt rung in an order all recognise: the others let her pass, eat and settle first and greet her with the calm signals of submission, or she passes, eats and settles after them and greets them so, and neither side has to fight it out each time. Intimates read it from who passes first when paths cross, who eats first, who takes the best spot, and who greets whom. Read with care: beliefs about the bodily signs of rank outrun the measured signs.

edits.by: Ben approved (9.03 am)
edits.was: This Pillar is the seniority you have been awarded within the group. This is the formal power you have to compel others and make decisions on behalf of the group. A small group may not have a rank structure, but it may formally attribute power unequally. Such power is distinct from that gained informally, or Popularity. Yet both may be the product of common consent, such as voting. The difference is the formalisation of the power, rather than being informal and thus needing to be negotiated.
edits.now: This Pillar is your felt place in the group's settled order of rank: how far others defer to you, give way to you and accept your decisions on behalf of the group. The rank may be conferred formally (an office, a title, a vote) or settled informally over time; what matters is that all recognise it and it need not be renegotiated each time. Deference here goes to your place, whatever others think of your skill.
edits.reason: Status covers rank settled formally or informally (H-to-E panel: formal conferred power has no chimpanzee counterpart, while the wordless core is a settled rank order); the Popularity cross-reference dropped and the boundary drawn against IncResp, which the status literature tends to merge with rank.

was.1: You have no formal power in the group and must seek permission to take any action.

now.10: Everyone in the group gives way to you, and no one acts against your decisions.

edits.by: Ben approved, 5 Nov 2026, 11.22 am (comparative psychologist's critique, docs/v3/sc-critique/)
edits.why: The present wording confuses the origin of precedence with its basis. Places are often won by skill or contribution, and in primates through kin and allies or through old contests. What makes precedence Status is that it has settled onto the place and is not fought out or held by fear now. The proposed wording from the brief is closer to the literature, but it needs 'present' fear (settled orders often began in force) and the kin and contest origins, or 'however you came by it' is undercut.

sources.source: de Waal, F., 1986, The integration of dominance and social bonding in primates, Quarterly Review of Biology 61: 459-479
sources.claim: Dominance is integrated with bonding through formalisation (unequivocal communication of status) and conditional reassurance; in some species status differences are attenuated and sharing replaces overt competition.

sources.source: Chapais, B., studies of rank acquisition and maintenance with kin support in captive Japanese macaques (1988 onward)

Status.subtitle: Your settled place in the pecking order
Status.summary: Rank is your felt rung in the group's settled order of precedence: how far you go first and take the first share, or go after others and take what is left. NormExp.name: Normative Expression (norm guarding)
NormExp.description: How strongly it strikes you as wrong when another member breaks from the group's settled ways, in act or by openly pressing to change them. It is felt indignation at a breach, not dislike of the person. Intimates read it from whether you pull the member up: an objection, mockery, a cold shoulder or shutting them out. Your own conformity and your openness to ideas are not part of it.

anchors.10: The smallest departure jars you at once as plainly wrong, and intimates see you pull the member up on the spot: a sharp word, a mocking laugh or a turned back.
anchors.1: A member doing or urging something different leaves you unmoved; nothing in you says it is wrong, and intimates see you let it pass.

NormExp.effect_on_other_pillars: NormExp has a delayed impact because it is assumed that your suppression or welcoming of ideas has already occurred. As with DivsExp, there is no assumption that any opinion has been acted on (although the scenario may play out that way).
NormExp.engagement: Where you feel that you can manage (minimise unwelcome or surprising) change, by using your power to reduce any propensity for others to suggest change. While high Rule-Keeping undermines Psychological Safety for others, it makes you personally feel safer.

pre_language.core: The bristle at one of the band doing a thing the wrong way. Its sign is the move to pull them up: a protest cry, a shove, a cold shoulder or exclusion. Two and three year olds already protest a puppet's wrong move (Rakoczy et al. 2008); Ju/'hoansi pull up breaches by criticism and mockery (Wiessner 2005); chimpanzees retaliate for their own losses but do not police third-party breaches (Riedl et al. 2012). Intimates read it from how she meets another's departure: with indignation and a rebuke, or with a shrug. Forager bands show the same bristle turned on upstarts and stingy members; in this model that egalitarian form is carried by Safety->Parity. The face here is the guarding of a ranked group's settled ways.

NormExp.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
NormExp.gloss: Indignation at breaches of the group's settled ways

excluded: Endorsing and defending the status quo yourself: expressing support for the group's settled ways and resisting change as such
Unwillingness to hear other members' suggestions (closed-mindedness; the old 1-anchor's 'listening intently')
Self-other asymmetry: feeling high DivsExp yourself while wanting to control others' DivsExp (only your own suggestions heard)
Feeling safer for enforcing (the 'and feeling safer for it' in the wordless version)
The groupthink framing ('similar to Group Think'; mindguards; pressure as a symptom of a cohesion-driven syndrome)
Negative reciprocity: paying back a wrong done to her (routed to NormExp by the Reciprocity proposal)

edits.why: The strongest human evidence for norm guarding comes from egalitarian foragers, and tightness tracks threat, not hierarchy. The deck placement can stand only if the face is defined as guarding a ranked group's settled ways, and the pre-language should say so instead of borrowing forager evidence for it.

OutResp.name: Outgoing Respect
OutResp.description: How far you feel the other members can be counted on to do their part in the shared work: each carries through what they take on and keeps their word about it, so you leave work in their hands without checking that they are doing it. It is reliability, not skill (Team Confidence): a willing but clumsy member rates high. It reads their part, not the return on your help (Reciprocity), whether anyone takes more than their due of shares, credit or say and makes it stick (Parity), or their verdict on your own conduct (Repute).

anchors.10: You leave any part of the work with any member and never check whether they are doing it; what they take on gets done and what they promise about it holds.
anchors.1: You check up on and chase others' work and redo what they skimp, expecting them to shirk, cut corners or go back on their word.

OutResp.effect_on_other_pillars: OutResp's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute.
OutResp.engagement: With competent and trustworthy people because you like being associated with 'winners', you admire and wish to model yourself off them, and they can help you to improve.

pre_language.core: Whether she can turn her back on them at a shared task. One who counts on her fellows leaves the watch, the carry or the young in their hands and goes about her own business without looking back; one who does not keeps glancing over, hovers at their work or takes it over herself. Intimates read it from how often she looks back, checks and takes over. The mechanism, trust calibrated to a partner's record, is the one chimpanzees show when they adjust trust to partners who have come through before (Engelmann et al. 2015); what sets this Pillar apart from Reciprocity is what the record is of: the partner's share of a joint task, not a favour returned to her. It is her reading of them; whether they turn their backs on her is a different thing and not read here.

Levelling.name: Levelling
Levelling.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
Levelling.description: How far you feel no one in the group sets themselves over you: makes you do, drop or endure things by force or fear; takes more than the band's ordinary share-out gives them, of food, credit or say, and makes it stick; or tilts how shares, turns and chances are handed out, or how a quarrel is settled, towards themselves or their favourites, passing you over. You go along of your own accord, unafraid, not shortchanged and not passed over. It is not rank (Rank), acceptance (Belonging), deference for what you bring (Esteem), the return on help (Reciprocity), whether others do their part of the work (Dependability) or the cost of showing yourself (Safety). A respected leader, a settled order you accept, an even-handed share-out that happens to leave you less this time, or the group together pulling up a breach of its ways leaves it high; a member you must appease, one who grabs and gets away with it, or one who hands out or settles in favour of his own lowers it. Where the group has spoken ways of deciding, being heard and having those ways applied to you as to anyone is the later, spoken form of the same reading.

anchors.10: No member or clique can make you do or drop anything by force or threat, no one takes more than their due and keeps it, and whoever hands out or settles things does so with no thumb on the scale. You move, take your share and go about your business in the strongest member's presence as freely as in anyone's.
anchors.1: One or a few members make you comply through force or fear, take more than their due and keep it, or hand out and settle things in favour of their own while you are passed over. You watch them warily, fall quiet when they come near, and let them have their way to head off their anger, or because objecting gets you nowhere.

pre_language.core: Freedom from a bully she must appease. The free animal moves, feeds and takes her share in the strongest member's presence without flinching or a glance at that member's mood; the coerced one tracks that member's moods, freezes on approach and does whatever heads off an attack. Intimates read it from whether she watches one particular member warily and shrinks or placates when that member comes near, while staying easy with everyone else, and whether, at a share-out, she is handed her portion in turn or watches the one dividing it feed his friends first and pass her by.

Levelling.descent: from rank perception, through coalitions of subordinates checking dominants. The capacity to read dominance is turned to levelling it (theory).
Levelling.gloss: No member bends you by force or fear

excluded: Coercion of the others: no one's will runs over the rest (witnessed or group-wide dominance)
Expectation that the others would stand with you against anyone who tried to push you about (coalitional check)
Leader's way rests on the others' going along, never imposed (consent-based legitimacy of leadership)
Appeal to a uniformly egalitarian ancestral band as the ground of the reading

edits.why: Anchor 10 says no one in the group can make you do or drop anything by force or threat. Read literally, it cannot be met in any group that enforces its ways, because collective sanctions such as mockery, a cold shoulder or shutting a member out (the pulling up named under NormExp) are threats. problems.where: description: 'Where the group has spoken ways of deciding, being heard and having those ways applied to you as to anyone is the later, spoken form of the same reading.'
problems.detail: Grocke et al. 2018 (supports) found children protested less only after they had agreed to a decision; being given a say and then overridden raised protest. 'Being heard' alone is partly contradicted by that result. Lind et al. 1990 (partly) supports a voice effect, but only on fairness judgements. 'The later, spoken form of the same reading' is a developmental or evolutionary claim with no source. Narrow it to having a say that counts, and drop 'later form'.

logic_status.common_sense: The felt side of coercion (watching one member warily, freezing on approach, placating to head off anger, moving freely in the strongest member's presence) is ordinary observation of fear of a particular person. A respected leader, or the group pulling up a breach together, leaving Parity high follows from Boehm 1993 (supports): followers level would-be dominants, not leadership as such. Grabbing that sticks rests on Peterson 1993 (supports). An even-handed share-out that leaves you less still leaving Parity high rests on Grocke et al. 2015 (supports). Bundling coercion, distributive grabs and tilted procedure into one reading is a modelling choice; Colquitt et al. 2001 shows the justice dimensions are distinct but intercorrelated, which does not contradict a single felt reading of 'someone sets themselves over me'. The logic leans on no animal inequity aversion, so the contested capuchin and chimpanzee results (Wynne 2004, Engelmann et al. 2017, Ritov et al. 2024) do not bear against it.

DivsExp.name: Diverse Expression (felt safety)
DivsExp.description: How safe you feel to show yourself in this group: to let a slip, a mood, a need or a disagreement show, or go about things your own way, expecting no put-down, mockery or rebuff for it. It is your reading of what showing yourself will cost you, not whether you speak up, whether your word carries weight (Esteem), whether you are wanted (Belonging), whether anyone pushes you about by force or fear (Parity), the verdict already held on your conduct (Repute), an open charge against your conduct (Face) or your own indignation at others' departures (Rule-Keeping).

anchors.10: You feel free to let slips, moods, needs and disagreements show as they come and to go about things your own way, expecting no one to pounce on them, laugh at them or turn away.
anchors.1: You feel that letting a slip, a mood, a plain need, a disagreement or a way of your own show would draw a put-down, so you scan faces before you move and keep your reactions masked.

DivsExp.effect_on_other_pillars: DivsExp has a delayed impact because it takes time for your contribution to either heard or ignored. Again, there is no assumption that it has been or will be acted on (although the scenario may play out that way).
DivsExp.engagement: Where you feel that your ideas will be welcomed and well-received. While related to IncResp (HCP), Expression is closer to a norm of Psychological Safety than being given specific respect for one's competence. Such a norm creates a warm, less hostile environment, which is distinct from cohesion: a close, friendly group can still make challenge feel risky.

Its reactive core, older than language, is latitude: feeling free to act differently from the group, or to start something new (a new way of doing a task, a new route), without being slapped down. Spoken suggestions are today's chief form of it.

anchors.1: You believe that your suggestions will be ignored, or not given due consideration even if (grudgingly) heard. You hold back from doing anything differently, expecting to be slapped down.

Reciprocity.name: Reciprocity
Reciprocity.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
Reciprocity.description: Your felt reading of whether help in this group comes back: what you give is returned, what you ask for is met. It holds until evidence moves it. It concerns the return on help, not whether others carry their part of shared work (Dependability), whether anyone takes more of a common take than their due (Parity), where you stand (Rank), whether the others want you among them (Belonging) or how they judge your conduct (Repute), though your name as a sharer (Repute) or as good for a return (Face) feeds the return. The culture's face sets where the return is looked for.

anchors.10: What you give comes back and what you ask for is met, as a matter of course; you count on the return without a second thought.
anchors.1: What you give is not returned and what you need goes unmet; you expect nothing back from anyone here.

Reciprocity.mechanics: Effects still assume help received (canon). The former IndRecip cards attach to the egalitarian Pillars and the former DirRecip cards to the hierarchical ones, so no card collides. A culture switch (HCP dominance drift, or its reverse) changes the face without resetting the level.
Reciprocity.effect_on_other_pillars: IndRecip's impact on other Pillars is based upon the assumption that assistance has been received. As such, it moves forward in time to the help having been rendered. The provision of assistance is not modelled because its impacts are less predictable. There is no Force card drawn if the character has provided assistance.

E.label: Return from the group
E.description: Help goes to whoever needs it, and the return comes from the group at large, not only from the one helped. It is conditional on being seen to share, not on a tally: one seen to share is given to, one seen to hoard is passed over, and whoever has a surplus is pressed to share on demand. Your reading is whether the group pays back what you put into it.

anchors.10: Whoever has gives to whoever needs; what you have put in comes back to you from any member when you are in need.
anchors.1: Giving goes into a hole: nothing comes back from anyone, those with a surplus hide it, and need goes unmet.

pre_language.core: Food handed over on demand within the band, with the return coming from whoever next has a surplus; those who hide food lose standing and are passed over. Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she hands her surplus to anyone who asks and asks anyone who has, or holds back from both.

E.engagement: Where you feel that the norm of IndRecip is strong because the group can adapt to challenges smoothly by moving effort to where it is most urgently needed, without needing to debate or cajole, and there is joy in feeling part of collective endeavour where no one prioritises self-interest or their own immediate tasking.
E.subtitle: Payback from the whole group
E.summary: Help goes to whoever needs it, and the return comes from the group at large, not only the one helped. It depends on being seen to share, not on a tally: sharers receive, hoarders are passed over, and surplus is pressed out on demand. The reading is whether the group repays what you put in.
E.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

H.label: Return from the partner
H.description: Help flows between particular partners who return it to each other. It is conditional on a return from the same partner: in kind between equals, or across rank, as favour and protection passed down for loyalty and service passed up. Your reading is whether your partners pay you back, not where you stand (Rank) or whether they do their part of the shared work (Dependability).

anchors.10: Every partner you help pays you back and those you ask deliver; whoever stands above you covers you and whoever stands below you backs you, each in turn.
anchors.1: Partners take and do not return; whoever stands above you leaves you uncovered and whoever stands below you will not back you; you expect no return from anyone you deal with.

pre_language.core: Grooming returned by the one groomed and support in fights traded between the same two (Schino and Aureli 2008; Schino 2007), with asymmetric exchange across rank: tolerance and protection down, support and deference up. Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she keeps giving to those who gave to her and turns from those who did not.

H.engagement: Where you feel that the norm of DirRecip is strong because the group can adapt to challenges smoothly by moving effort to where it is most urgently needed, by trusting each other's word (assuming there are favours that each can do for each other); there is joy in feeling part of an endeavour where promises to return favours are always kept, and your efforts end up being recognised and returned; this version of trust is more honouring a deal, rather than being trusted to carry out tasks reliably (as per IncResp and OutResp).
H.subtitle: Payback from your own partners
H.summary: Help flows between particular partners who return it to each other. The return must come from the same partner: in kind between equals, or across rank, with favour and protection passing down for loyalty and service passing up. The reading is whether your partners pay you back. It is not Rank or Dependability.
H.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

pre_language.core: The felt return on sharing: grooming that is returned by those groomed (Schino and Aureli 2008) and forager food handed over on demand that comes back from the band's next kill (Peterson 1993). Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she hands over on request and asks as of right, expecting the return, or hesitates, hoards and goes without rather than ask.

excluded: Her own readiness to give help (helping behaviour, positive-reciprocity disposition)
Her own readiness to seek help
Negative reciprocity (returning harm for harm)
Costs of helping and of offering (distraction from own tasks, risk of rejection)
The canon that a culture is dominated by one face and not both, and the mapping of unconditional help to egalitarian and conditional help to hierarchical cultures
Evolutionary claims: that unconditional reciprocity distinguishes human from primate collaboration, that direct reciprocity is more common in primates, and that bonobos trade sex for favours
The word unconditional for the egalitarian face
Others' reliability in shared work (doing their part, keeping their word)

edits.why: The Levelling pointer 'whether shares of a common take are even' disagrees with Levelling, which is lowered only by someone taking more than the group's own reckoning gives them, and stays high under an accepted settled order (where Status gives first share). Otherwise consistent with OutResp and Status and with the generalised versus direct reciprocity literature (Sahlins; Nowak and Sigmund 2005).

edits.why: 1. The egalitarian face is held in two copies that disagree: 'membership in good standing as a sharer' against 'membership and standing'. The second leans on 'standing', the name of the Popularity/Status axis, and so points towards Status, which the base text excludes. 2. The egalitarian face makes the return conditional on being known as a sharer, which borders Belonging (egalitarian face: one of their own in good standing) and Repute (verdict on whether you deal fairly and pull your weight), yet the base text names neither; Repute names Reciprocity, so the boundary is one-sided. 3. The generic anchor 10 opens 'Help goes where it is needed', the egalitarian face's wording, so it misreads under the hierarchical face, where help goes to partners. Fixes: one wording for the egalitarian condition, without 'standing', stored once; two boundary clauses; a face-neutral anchor 10. The faces otherwise match the literature as I know it: demand sharing and generalised reciprocity with sharing contingent on a name as a sharer (Woodburn 1982; Peterson 1993; Sahlins 1972; Nowak and Sigmund 1998 on indirect reciprocity) for the egalitarian face, and balanced reciprocity and patron-client exchange (Sahlins 1972; Scott 1972) for the hierarchical face. References from memory, not checked here.

problems.where: faces.E.description: "It is conditional on being seen to share, not on a tally" (and the same in faces.E.summary)
problems.detail: Allen-Arave, Gurven and Hill 2008 (supports) find Ache transfers contingent on past giving between households, even among kin. Jaeggi and Gurven 2013 (supports) find reciprocity contributes to forager food sharing independently of kinship and scrounging. Neither shows a conscious tally, but both show contingency on the partner's past giving, so a flat "not on a tally" overstates it. Soften.

problems.where: pre_language.core: "forager food handed over on demand that comes back from the band's next kill (Peterson 1993)"
problems.detail: The checker rates Peterson 'partly': demand sharing and the pressure on holders are supported, but the return-from-the-group framing is the model's, and nothing about the return coming from the next kill was found. Do not hang it on Peterson.

problems.where: faces.H.pre_language.core: "support in fights traded between the same two (... Schino 2007), with asymmetric exchange across rank: tolerance and protection down, support and deference up"
problems.detail: Schino 2007 has no checker verdict, and the claim of asymmetric primate exchange across rank has no checked source. Only Schino and Aureli 2008 (grooming reciprocation) is checked.

problems.where: description: "though your name as a sharer (Repute) or as good for a return (Face) feeds the return"
problems.detail: Face is defined elsewhere (Repute, Esteem H, Safety) as an open charge or being caught out before those who count. It is not one's name as good for a return. The gloss contradicts that definition.

logic_status.common_sense: H face's exchange across rank in the description (favour and protection down, loyalty and service up): safe as common sense of patronage, though no checked source backs it. The mechanics line is design. The anchors are plain readings of the definition.

Belonging.description: How far you feel the others want you among them: whether they make room for you and draw you in, or leave you at the edge. It is their acceptance of you, read from how they treat you, not whether they defer to you for skill or contribution (Esteem), where you stand in the order (Rank) or how they judge your conduct (Repute). The culture's face sets what the acceptance rests on.

anchors.10: Others make room for you on sight and draw you into whatever is going on; you never doubt that you are wanted here.
anchors.1: Gatherings form without you and you are left at the edge; you doubt that anyone wants you here.

Belonging.effect_on_other_pillars: Popularity's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute.

E.label: Wanted as one of their own in good standing
E.description: The others want you among them as one of their own in good standing: you pull with the group as far as you are able and do not feed on it. The acceptance does not rise or fall with your output or with any place in an order, but it is not unconditional: a member who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others is edged out. You read it from how the group as a whole treats you.

anchors.10: Others make room for you and draw you in as a matter of course, and have done so through good seasons and bad; only shirking, cheating or turning on the group would change it.
anchors.1: Gatherings form without you and you are left at the edge: they treat you as a freeloader or an outsider, not as one of their own.

pre_language.core: Let into the huddle after a failed hunt as readily as after a good one, so long as she still pulls with the band; the one who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others is edged out, however able.

E.engagement: Where you feel comfortable and accepted by the group members, who 'have your back' and will support you in the event of any difficulties, and where you enjoy the power of influence (informal leadership).

E.summary: The others want you among them as one of their own in good standing, as long as you pull with the group and do not feed on it. H.description: The others keep you among them so long as you keep to what your place in the order calls for, high or low, and do not step out of line. The acceptance is real but conditional on keeping the place, not on the place itself (Rank). You read it from how they treat you while you keep it and from the standing threat of being dropped.

anchors.10: You have kept your place and the others keep you among them: at every gathering a place is made for you, whether high or low, as a matter of course.
anchors.1: You have stepped out of line and been dropped, or were never given a place at all: gatherings form without you and you are kept at the edge.

pre_language.core: Kept in the group, at whatever rank she holds, for as long as she does what her place calls for; the moment she oversteps, the others turn on her or shut her out, and she feels the edge of that long before it happens.

Belonging.gloss: How far the others want you among them

pre_language.core: Being let into the huddle or kept out of it, time after time. The others shift to make a place, share, groom and turn towards her, or close ranks, turn away and leave her at the fringe, and keep doing so. Intimates read it from whether she moves freely into the middle of the group or hovers at its edge, watching for a gap.

excluded: Uniqueness and authenticity: being valued for what makes you different, and free to be yourself in the group
Mattering: being missed when absent, being important to and depended on by the others
Being valued for your contribution (perceived value, competence- or contribution-based respect)
Being 'one of us': group identification, solidarity and centrality of membership
Inclusion in decision-making, information and influence networks

elaboration_notes: Elaboration: when low Belonging comes from being shut out, the reaction may carry hostility towards those who did it, even with no one watching (rejected people turn aggressive towards the rejecters and towards neutral others: Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001). The hostility belongs in the elaboration, not on a card. When the exclusion is public and reads as a slight to her good name, the Reputation expansion carries the flare and the urge to hit back.

The acceptance does not rise or fall with your output or with any place in an order, but it is not unconditional: a member who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others is edged out. You read liking from the group as a whole.

- 1: You have stepped out of line and been dropped, or were never given a place at all: gatherings form without you and you are kept at the edge.

edits.why: 1. The general definition carries copies of both faces and their anchors, giving three pairs of anchors. Fix: keep only the general paragraph and the general anchors (the last pair). 2. The stored face_E disagrees with itself and with its neighbours. It requires that you be 'no burden' on the group, and its anchor 1 has you treated 'as a burden'. Yet the same face says acceptance 'does not rise or fall with your output'. Repute and Face also put a share that falls short for want of skill on Prestige's ground, with only a failure of will counting against the member. A sick, old or unskilled member is a burden but is not edged out. The copied version, 'pull with the group as far as you are able and do not feed on it', with 'freeloader' in anchor 1, keeps the condition on will, as Boehm (1999) describes egalitarian groups sanctioning freeloaders. 3. Stored face_E anchor 10 says 'nothing short of your turning against the group would change it'. That contradicts the description, where a member who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others is edged out. The copied anchor ('only shirking, cheating or turning on the group would change it') agrees with it. 4. 'You read liking from the group as a whole' swaps in liking for acceptance. The general definition reads acceptance from treatment, and Repute treats liking as something that only colours the verdict on conduct. The sociometer literature also frames this as relational value and inclusion rather than liking (Leary and Baumeister 2000). Fix: read it from how the group as a whole treats you. 5. The hierarchical face agrees with Status ('conditional on keeping the place, not on the place itself') and with NormExp, Face and Repute. No change.

era.why: Being drawn in or left at the edge, through approach, grooming, proximity and exclusion, is the core of primate social inclusion and ostracism.

Prestige.name: Prestige
Prestige.description: How far the others defer to you freely for what you bring: they turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice. It is not whether they want you among them (Belonging), your rung in the settled order (Rank) or their verdict on your conduct (Repute). The culture's face sets how far the deference reaches.

anchors.10: Whenever your kind of skill or contribution counts, the others turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice.
anchors.1: No one asks you, watches you or copies you; when your kind of skill or contribution is needed they turn to someone else.

Prestige.effect_on_other_pillars: You respond to the current assessment of others' respect for you.
Prestige.engagement: Where you feel that others have a high opinion of your competence and trustworthiness: you feel valued and understood; you feel that others regard you to be a legitimate and useful member of the group; your identity as belonging to this group is consistent with others' appraisal of you.

pre_language.core: Being the one others watch, copy and seek out: eyes on her hands, bodies drawn near while she works, problems brought to her, her way of doing things taken up, the giver sought as a partner; as children and apes attend to and copy skilled or much-attended models, and as the most giving members of a group are sought out and honoured. Intimates read it from who gets watched, copied and sought, and who is passed over when a task of her kind comes up.

era.why: Being watched and copied for a valued skill has non-verbal analogues: chimpanzees preferentially copy older, successful models (Kendal et al. 2015); Henrich and Gil-White (2001) tie prestige to cultural learning, which preceded full language, though advice-taking is a later spoken form.

Prestige.subtitle: Deference for what you bring
Prestige.summary: How far the others defer to you freely for what you bring: they turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice. It is not whether they want you among them (Belonging), your rung in the settled order (Rank) or their verdict on your conduct (Repute). The culture's face sets how far the deference reaches.
Prestige.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

E.label: Looked to for what you bring, kept modest
E.description: How far you feel the others turn to you freely for what you bring the band: skill, knowledge, generosity, a good eye for the venture in hand. They watch how you do it, copy you, follow your lead on the matter in hand and bring you their problems, while you stay one of them: the deference gives you no right to command, and it lasts only while what you bring does and while you carry it modestly. Being shown up as clumsy or mistaken on a matter of skill, or as falling short on your share for want of skill rather than will, lowers it; falling short for want of will is Repute's ground. It is not whether they want you among them (Belonging), not freedom from being pushed about (Parity), not the return on your help (Reciprocity) and not their verdict on your conduct (Repute).

anchors.10: Whenever your kind of skill counts, the others look to you, copy how you do it and follow your lead on it for the day, and still rib you as one of them.
anchors.1: No one watches, copies or follows you on anything; when your kind of skill is needed they turn to someone else.

pre_language.core: The good hunter whose way of tracking the young copy and whose call on where to go is followed for the day, while his meat is still mocked as poor.

E.subtitle: Looked to for your skill, modestly
E.summary: How far the others turn to you freely for what you bring the band: skill, knowledge, generosity, a good eye for the venture. They watch, copy, follow your lead on the matter in hand and bring you problems, while you stay one of them. It gives no right to command and lasts only while what you bring does and you carry it modestly.

H.label: Deferred to for what you bring
H.description: How far you feel the others defer to you freely for what you bring the group: skill, knowledge or contribution it values, generosity included. They watch how you do it, copy you, bring you problems, take your advice, hand you decisions and jobs that matter and take your word on them. The deference is given, not owed to any place in a rank order (Rank). Being handed a decision or a job because of what you bring is part of it; being shown up before others as clumsy or mistaken on a matter of skill, or as falling short on your share for want of skill rather than will, lowers it. Whether the others count you a fair sharer who will carry your share of the work is not (Repute), though one generous act can feed both; nor is whether anyone of standing has openly charged you with wronging people or dodging your share (Face); and neither is whether help you give comes back to you (Reciprocity). It fades once what you bring does; any precedence that has by then settled into your place is Rank, not Esteem.

anchors.10: Whenever your kind of skill or contribution counts, the others turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice.
anchors.1: No one asks you, watches you or copies you; when your kind of skill or contribution is needed they turn to someone else.

pre_language.core: Being the one others watch, copy and seek out: eyes on her hands, bodies drawn near while she works, problems brought to her, her way of doing things taken up, the giver sought as a partner; as children and apes attend to and copy skilled or much-attended models, and as the most giving members of a group are sought out and honoured. Intimates read it from who gets watched, copied and sought, and who is passed over when a task of her kind comes up.

forces.name: Making Fetch Happen
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, and after a knock one of them comes and sits with me, my bracing eases; I expect a slip, a mood or a disagreement of mine to be taken as coming from one of their own, and my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and no one comes to me after a knock, I expect a slip or a disagreement of mine to be met as an outsider's would be, with a rebuff, and I mask myself and brace: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: Consolation by a valued partner lowers stress behaviour in chimpanzees after aggression (Fraser, Stahl and Aureli 2008), and it comes mostly from partners with valuable relationships; a member drawn in as one of their own has such partners to come to her. A member who is wanted expects her exposure to be borne as one of their own; one left at the edge expects it to be held against her. Felt safety in teams is a shared reading that interpersonal risk is acceptable (Edmondson 1999).

pre_language.decrement: When others leave her at the edge, she watches faces, masks her reactions and braces for a snap.

forces.name: Friends at my back
forces.increment_logic: When I feel the others want me among them, I sense they would close round me if anyone tried to push me about, and my sense that no one can lord it over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and no one seeks me out, I feel I would stand alone if someone pushed me about, and my sense that no one can lord it over me falls.
forces.explanation: Felt protection from domination rests on expected coalitional support, and being bonded into the group is the felt basis of that expectation; an isolated member is exposed. Elaboration: when the low reading comes from being shut out, her reaction may show hostility, aimed readily at whoever she deals with next, even someone who has done nothing to her, and withheld only from those who treat her warmly (Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001); if the exclusion is public and stands as an open charge that she wronged someone or let the group down on her share, the Reputation expansion (Face) carries that flare.

pre_language.decrement: When others leave her on her own, she shrinks when a forceful member nears, with no one to run to, and her sense of no bully sinks.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from expected backing to the member's felt sense that no one can lord it over her, and the line "an isolated member is exposed". Both are safe because a felt reading follows expected support, and the sources supply the support itself. Literature: rank and file combining against would-be dominants (Boehm 1993, partly); grooming bonds exchanged for agonistic support (Seyfarth 1977, supports; Schino and Aureli 2008, partly). The elaboration says that exclusion may bring hostility towards neutral others, withheld from one who treats her warmly. That matches Twenge et al. 2001 (supports), and "may" is the right strength given the contested replication record. One caveat that is not a failure: Seyfarth's model concerns grooming up the hierarchy for support from dominants, so in a deck E card it backs the coalitional support step, not an egalitarian setting as such.

forces.name: One of us, so it comes back
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I feel surer that what I put in will come back from the group and that what I need will be met: my sense that help comes back to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and I am left at the edge, I feel that what I give goes into a hole and that my needs would go unmet: my sense that help comes back to me falls.
forces.explanation: In the return-from-the-group face, help goes to whoever in the group needs it, and someone the others treat as an outsider stands outside that giving. Being wanted as one of their own in good standing is the felt sign that she is among those the group's giving reaches, so her need will be met; being left at the edge is the sign that she stands outside that reach and will be passed over. Her name as a sharer is a separate route (Bad Name, Empty Hands). People expect generalised returns from their own group and not from outsiders (bounded generalised reciprocity: Yamagishi and Kiyonari 2000); carrying that from group membership to graded acceptance within one group is an extension, so keep the step modest.

pre_language.increment: When others seek her out and draw her in, she reaches for a share of what they have without hesitation, expecting it to be handed over, and her sense that giving comes back grows.
pre_language.decrement: When others leave her at the edge, she hangs back from the food and holds what she has close, expecting nothing to come her way, and her sense that giving comes back sinks.

reactive_test.reason: An inference from emotionally weighted treatment (being drawn in or shut out) to expecting to be given to, with an obvious pre-language form in sharing food.

logic_status.common_sense: Carrying bounded generalised reciprocity over from group membership to graded acceptance within one group, so that a member left at the edge is treated as partly outside the group's giving. The explanation states that this is an extension and asks for a modest step. It is safe at that strength because being left out is the plain in-group sign of being treated as an outsider. Need-based giving within the face is the model's definition of that face, not a claim about the world.

forces.name: Open or masked
forces.explanation: Whether feeling safe to show myself draws the others closer depends on what I would be showing them. Circumstance one: what shows is ordinary, moods, owned slips and disagreements aired for the group's sake. HIGH: I let them show, the others read me as one of their own and draw me in, so my Belonging rises. LOW: braced and masked, I come across as aloof, and they leave me at the edge of the talk, so my Belonging falls. Circumstance two: what I have to show is mostly a run of needs and complaints I lean on the others to carry while giving back less than I could, and they have begun to read it as feeding on them. HIGH: I go on letting them show, I read more and more as feeding on them instead of pulling with them, and they edge away, so my Belonging falls. LOW: braced and masked, I keep those needs to myself; with nothing new to carry, they stop edging away and let me back into the talk, so my Belonging rises. Someone already wanted among them is borne with longer, and needs she cannot help are borne as one of their own. Masked expression lowers a partner's rapport and wish to affiliate (Butler et al. 2003), and disclosure draws liking (Collins and Miller 1994), for circumstance one.

pre_language.explanation: When she does her share alongside the others, showing her moods and fumbles freely draws them to her, while going still and masked leaves her on the edge. When the others have begun to turn from her constant wants and complaints, showing more of them makes them turn further away, while keeping them hidden lets them come back to her and make room for her again.

reactive_test.reason: Both directions are others' felt reactions to what she shows, read by her as warmth or coldness, with no worked-out plan involved.

problems.where: framework: "excessive reassurance seeking draws rejection (Coyne; Joiner and colleagues)"
problems.detail: The cited Joiner link resolves to Joiner et al. 2001 on how specific reassurance seeking is to depression. The checker rated it not in source. The claim is backed only by the sorted Starr and Davila 2008 meta-analysis (partly: r = .14, a small effect, in depression-linked dyads). Cite that instead and state the effect as small.

problems.where: explanation, circumstance two LOW: "braced and masked, I keep those needs to myself; with nothing new to carry, they stop edging away and let me back into the talk, so my Belonging rises."
problems.detail: No source shows that holding needs back reverses rejection. Starr and Davila show only that reassurance seeking goes with rejection. Butler et al. 2003 (supports) show that masked expression lowers a partner's rapport, which cuts against Belonging rising when she masks. Being let back into the talk within minutes is also a slow repair effect, outside a card's timescale. Make this branch hold Belonging steady. If the rulebook needs a direction for every discretionary branch, drop circumstance two LOW and let circumstance one govern.

problems.where: explanation, circumstance two HIGH: "they edge away, so my Belonging falls"
problems.detail: The rejection effect is small (r = .14). Say they edge away a little so the step stays modest.

logic_status.common_sense: "Someone already wanted among them is borne with longer, and needs she cannot help are borne as one of their own": safe as ordinary experience, and in line with the will-versus-skill line in Delton et al. 2012 (checked for Face, not cited here). The step in circumstance two from heavy needs to being read as feeding on them is the model's reading of the reassurance-seeking literature.

forces.name: Mistakes in the open
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a slip or a disagreement show, I sense that troubles with the venture come out where the group can deal with them, and I feel surer it can pull the venture off.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I sense that slips and doubts are being hidden around me as well as by me, and I feel less sure the group can pull the venture off.
forces.explanation: Psychological safety lets errors and disagreements surface early, which is how teams learn and correct course; in Edmondson's (1999) teams it worked on performance through that learning behaviour. Edmondson measured safety as a belief the team shares. A member's own felt safety is one sign of whether that climate holds around her, so it carries into her confidence in the group's capability. Her sense that others hide their slips too is an inference from her own masking, so keep the step modest.

pre_language.increment: When she is loose among them and her fumbles on the shared venture draw help rather than jeers, she sees fumbles mended as they happen and goes at the venture with confidence.
pre_language.decrement: When she is braced and hides her fumbles, she sees others hide theirs too, and the venture feels shakier to her.

reactive_test.reason: The felt climate drives the reading, but the step from her own safety to the group's capacity to correct itself can slide towards reasoning about group process.

forces.name: Free to scoff, free of bullies
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a disagreement show, I bristle or scoff at anyone who starts to push me about, help themselves to more than their due, or tilt a share-out or a turn towards themselves or their favourites, and when others take up my scoff the move is checked: I feel no one here could set themselves over me without an answer from us, and my sense of Parity rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I let a pushy member's demands, grabs and favouritism pass without a murmur and take what is handed to me, and I feel myself made to go along: my sense of Parity falls.
forces.explanation: The everyday tools of levelling are ridicule, criticism and open objection, and they work because they are collective: Ju/'hoansi put-downs of big-shot behaviour escalate across the camp to harsh criticism and withheld sharing (Wiessner 2005; Boehm 1993). A member who feels safe to show herself uses them on reflex; where others take them up, force, grabbing and favouritism lose their grip on her. A lone scoff that no one takes up does not check a dominant, so set the increment small where the others stay silent; expected backing is carried by E:Belonging->Parity. The favouritism limb follows Q5: preschoolers protest an unequal split more when a rigged procedure produced it than when a fair one did (Grocke, Rossano and Tomasello 2015).

forces.name: Need shown, need met
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a need show, I let it show, and seeing it met I feel surer that what I put into this group comes back.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and keep my needs masked, I only hint at them; the hints go unnoticed and nothing comes, and I read the silence as a refusal: my sense that help in this group comes back falls.
forces.explanation: Felt safety lets a member show her needs, and the help that answers them confirms the return. A braced member only hints at hers. People overrate how plainly others can read their inner states (illusion of transparency: Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec 1998), so she takes her hint as a request, sees nothing come, and reads the silence as a refusal. People also underestimate how readily others help when asked directly (Flynn and Lake 2008), so a member who shows a need is met more often than she expects, while one who masks it never learns her estimate was too low. Both findings come from studies of strangers and pairs; carrying them into a standing group is an extension, so keep both steps modest, and keep the decrement small where she has not hinted at a need at all.

forces.name: Reading the welcome through my own warmth
forces.increment_logic: When this group feels part of who I am, the small signs (a nod, a seat kept, a glance my way) read to me as welcome for one of their own, and my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, the same small signs read as mere politeness and the gaps read as edging me out, as if I were an outsider, and my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: Most belonging cues in a small group are ambiguous, and people read them in line with how they themselves stand. The sociometer gauges felt relational value from such cues (Leary and Baumeister 2000), and ambiguous cues are read in the direction the reader expects or wants (Kunda 1990; Downey and Feldman 1996 for expected rejection). Those works concern expectation and desire, not investment, so the step from her own investment to that reading is a proposal on common sense. A person for whom the group is part of who she is gives the others the benefit of the doubt. A person on her way out reads coolness into the same scene, and finds in it a felt reason for going. Primates that move to the edge of a troop are approached and groomed less, so drawing back is confirmed by what she then sees, but the card covers only the re-reading. Her own investment colours how she reads their acceptance of her as one of their own; how they judge her conduct is Repute's ground, and the card moves only her reading of the others' treatment, not the treatment itself.

pre_language.decrement: Drifting away from the band, she reads the others' glances as indifferent and sees groups forming without her. Her feeling of being wanted among them falls.

reactive_test.reason: Mood-congruent reading of social cues is an immediate emotional inference, with a clear pre-language form in approach and edge-drifting.

forces.name: Bringing herself in, or bracing
forces.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, I bring my whole self into it, and the faces around me read as open rather than judging: I feel safer letting slips, moods, needs and disagreements show.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have withdrawn into myself and am on my way out of this group, the same faces read as watchful and ready to mock: I mask my reactions, braced for a put-down, and feel less safe to let them show.
forces.explanation: Kahn (1990) defines engagement and disengagement as two movements of the self: expressing it in the role, or withdrawing and defending it. The established path runs the other way: across 136 samples, psychological safety is an antecedent of engagement (Frazier et al. 2017). This feedback path is a proposal resting on Kahn's account: a self that is defending braces and reads neutral faces as threat, while a self that is expressing is loose and reads the same faces as open. Mood-congruent perception has been offered for it, but Engagement is investment, not mood, so that route applies only through the enthusiasm that goes with investment. Keep the card smaller than Safety's evidence cards. I considered Inverse (an invested member has more to lose, so feels more exposed) but rejected it as the default, because Kahn treats self-expression and engagement as one movement; that exposure effect belongs on a scene card about how a shown disagreement is received.

forces.name: Thrown in, the venture looks winnable
forces.increment_logic: When I am thrown into this group heart and effort, I feel buoyed, and what we manage feels like a sign of what we can do: I feel more sure that we, as we stand, can pull off the venture we have taken on.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have withdrawn from this group and am half out of the door, I feel flat, and the same showing looks like the limit of what we can do: I feel less sure that we, as we stand, can pull off the venture we have taken on.
forces.explanation: Her own investment carries a feeling (enthusiasm or flatness), and that feeling seeps unbidden into her reading of the group's capability for the venture still ahead. The Affect Infusion Model describes the route: mood colours judgements she builds from scratch, whether by quick heuristics or by working them through, and colours least those she simply recalls or makes with a set aim in view (Forgas 1995). Salanova, Llorens and Schaufeli (2011) report a gain spiral over time in which engagement and enthusiasm feed back into efficacy beliefs, so the loop runs from engagement to felt prospects as well as the reverse. Most of that evidence concerns a member's belief in her own capability; its spread to the group's capability is less directly tested. Effort justification (Aronson and Mills 1959) is sometimes offered as extra support, but field studies of real initiations have given weak or contrary results, so it is not relied on here. Because Team Confidence also feeds Engagement, the two form a positive loop; the brake must come from Team Confidence evidence cards (setbacks, missed goals), and the increment here should be modest.

pre_language.decrement: Withdrawn and hanging back, she sees the band fumble, and the venture ahead looks beyond it: her sense of the band's prospects falls.

reactive_test.reason: Mood seeping into a felt sense of what the group can do is an emotional inference, not a worked-out forecast.
