forces.name: Inside the coalition
forces.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, it feels like ours to defend, and I feel ready to stand with the rest against anyone who throws their weight about; a forceful member no longer looks able to make me do or drop anything, or to take more than their due and keep it: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have drawn back and am on my way out of this group, it no longer feels worth a stand, and I would sooner keep my head down than face anyone down; a forceful member looms larger and I give way to their mood: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls.
forces.explanation: In forager bands, the absence of a bully rests on a levelling coalition of the rest, ready to check a would-be dominant (Boehm 1993). Feeling free of coercion therefore depends partly on her own readiness to join that check. Commitment to a group raises the will to speak up and resist when things go wrong, while low commitment turns members towards exit or silent neglect (Hirschman 1970; Rusbult and colleagues 1988). When Engagement is high the group feels like hers to defend, so a forceful member feels unable to make her comply. When it is low nothing here seems worth a stand, and the same forcefulness feels like a threat she must appease. Caution: a member with somewhere else to go depends less on the group, and dependence is what gives others power over her (Emerson 1962), so set the decrement small or nil where her exit is ready and cheap. Whether the others would back her is a separate matter, carried by Friends at my back (Belonging). Parity here is her own felt exposure to force or fear, and leaves aside whether she likes or rates the forceful member.

pre_language.increment: Drawn into the band, she stands among the others when a forceful member swaggers, feels them at her side and goes on with her business. Her sense that no one can push her about rises.
pre_language.decrement: Pulled to the band's edge, she watches the forceful member warily, goes still when it comes near and gives way, feeling no one at her back. Her sense that no one can push her about falls.

reactive_test.reason: Felt safety or wariness in a forceful member's presence, read through felt allies, is a pre-language reaction.

problems.detail: Emerson 1962 was never checked. The claim can stand only as common sense, without the citation.

problems.detail: The decrement line describes a member on her way out, but the Caution says to set the decrement small or nil exactly where exit is ready. logic_status.common_sense: The step from Boehm's collective levelling coalition to one member's felt freedom from coercion; a withdrawn member who cannot leave keeping her head down; a member with a cheap way out having less to lose from defiance.

forces.name: Trusting those I am in it with
forces.increment_logic: When I am thrown into this group, I read the others warmly, and the way they carry their part looks dependable: I feel more confident that they will do what they take on.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have withdrawn from this group, I read the others coolly, and the one task let drop is what stays with me: I feel less confident that they will do what they take on.
forces.explanation: Two felt routes. Mood congruence: investment brings warmth, and warmth colours quick judgements of whether others will keep their word (Forgas 1995). That route acts in the moment. Sampling works over many plays: an engaged member keeps relying on others, so a single let-down is soon corrected by tasks carried through; a disengaged member stops relying on them, so the last let-down stands as the verdict (Denrell 2005). The card moves reliability only, not her reading of the group's capability (Team Confidence). One caution: the sucker effect (Kerr 1983) shows that a member who is putting in a lot reacts sharply when a partner coasts. That reaction is real and acts as a brake, but it is driven by seeing the coasting, so it belongs on a Dependability evidence card, not here.

pre_language.increment: Bound up in the band, she leaves tasks in others' hands and sees them done, and each task carried through sticks: her trust that those around her will do their part rises.
pre_language.decrement: Withdrawn from the band, she stops leaving tasks with others, and the last task dropped is what she carries away: her trust that they will do their part falls.

reactive_test.reason: Warmth-coloured trust and the lingering of the last let-down are emotional inferences from weighted evidence, with a plain pre-language form.

problems.detail: The checker notes that the affect infusion model predicts weaker infusion, or even reversals, under motivated processing. Judging whether a teammate she depends on will deliver is a likely case of motivated processing, so a flat mood-bias claim goes beyond the source. Add the hedge.

problems.detail: This phrase draws on the Denrell sampling route, which the explanation itself says works over many plays. Cards are felt reactions within minutes, so the line should rest on the in-the-moment mood route.

logic_status.common_sense: Being invested in a group goes with a warmer mood towards its members, and drawing back with a cooler one. This is safe only as a modest default, because an invested member can also be frustrated.

forces.name: One of us, so paid back
forces.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, I pour my time and effort into it, and what comes my way reads as the group paying back what I have put in: my sense that help here comes back to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I know I have been holding back my time and effort, and when I am in need I expect the group to pass me over as I have passed it by: my sense that help here comes back to me falls.
forces.explanation: In egalitarian sharing the return comes from the group, and it still follows each member's standing as a giver: households that give more receive more (Gurven 2004), even where demand sharing gives every member some claim on a surplus (Peterson 1993). Engagement is the felt size of her stake and effort in the group. When it is high she counts herself a sharer the group gives to, and reads ambiguous cues of others' giving as return for what she has put in. When it is low she knows she has held back and expects to be passed over, as a hoarder is. Whether the others want her among them is a separate route (One of us, so it comes back), and so is what they say of her as a sharer (Bad Name, Empty Hands). The card moves her reading of the group's return; it keeps no tally of particular debts.

pre_language.increment: Bound up in the band, she shares freely and feels the band's food and help come round to her in turn. Her sense that what she gives comes back rises.
pre_language.decrement: Loosened from the band, she keeps to herself and, when hungry, hangs back expecting nothing to be passed her way. Her sense that what she gives comes back falls.

reactive_test.reason: An inference from emotionally weighted information about her own standing among the sharers, of a kind a band-living animal could form without words; no reckoning of returns is involved.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, I feel myself one of us, a known sharer, and what comes my way reads as the group paying back what I put in; my sense that help here comes back to me rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I feel myself the one who holds back, the kind the group passes over, and when I am in need I expect nothing to come my way; my sense that help here comes back to me falls.
ripple_was.explanation: In egalitarian sharing, the return comes from the group and is contingent on being a member in good standing: households that give more receive more (Gurven 2004), and demand sharing presses those with a surplus to give to whoever counts as one of us (Peterson 1993). Engagement is the felt size of her stake and presence in the group. When it is high she feels herself a sharer the group gives to, and reads ambiguous cues of others' giving as return for what she has put in. When it is low she feels herself on the hoarder's side of the line and expects to be passed over. What moves is her reading of the group's return, not any tally of particular debts.

problems.where: explanation: 'households that give more receive more (Gurven 2004), even where demand sharing gives every member some claim on a surplus (Peterson 1993)'
problems.detail: This is the card's core evidence, and neither Gurven 2004 nor Peterson 1993 is in the checked literature. The two sources that were checked (Tomasello and colleagues 2012; Roberts 2005) appear nowhere in the explanation.

problems.where: framework: 'Interdependence hypothesis; stakeholder theory of cooperation' against the explanation
problems.detail: The framework and the checked sources rest on stake theory: those who depend on her have a direct interest in her welfare and help her. The explanation instead argues contingent giving, where givers receive more. The cited literature backs a different mechanism from the one the text argues.

problems.where: literature use of Tomasello and colleagues 2012 and Roberts 2005
problems.detail: Both are theoretical evolutionary accounts. The checker notes that extending them to Engagement in a present-day small group is the model's step. Say so.

logic_status.common_sense: An invested member reads ambiguous cues of others' giving as return for her effort. A member who has held back expects to be passed over. Both are ordinary self-assessments of standing as a giver, and both are safe if kept modest.

forces.name: Circle the Wagons
forces.explanation: Whether the venture's prospects draw the others round her depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Circumstance one (the default), the trouble is seen as inside the group or no source is named. HIGH: the venture going well, the others are easy with each other and with her, make room and draw her in, so her Belonging rises (runs as Reinforce). LOW: the venture failing, the others grow short with each other, small cliques form, and she is left at the edge of the talk, so her Belonging falls. In the egalitarian face acceptance holds through good seasons and bad, so keep this branch modest, and smallest for a member long drawn in; being blamed herself for the failure is Repute's ground (Pointing Fingers), not this card's. Circumstance two, the trouble is seen as coming from outside (a rival group, an outside body, a setback from outside such as lost funding or a forced change of ground), and the group still sees a fight worth making. LOW: the others close ranks against it and draw her in as one of us, so her Belonging rises (runs as Inverse). HIGH: the outside threat looks easily met, the huddle loosens and her place returns to its ordinary level, so her Belonging slips back down, by no more than an earlier huddle raised it; with no such rise, the step is nil. External threat binds a group only when it falls on all of them and a joint effort seems able to meet it (Stein 1976); where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one. Newcomers gain least from the outside-threat branch and lose most in the inside branch.

pre_language.explanation: Where the band huddles when things go badly and she is still half an outsider, a faltering venture has them gathering close and pulling her in among them, while a venture going well lets them drift back to leaving her on the edge. Where the band turns on whoever seems to drag, a faltering venture may leave her at the edge, while a venture going well sees them make room for her again.

reactive_test.reason: Huddling under threat and turning on a weak member are both felt group reactions she reads directly as being drawn in or edged out.

critique_was.explanation: Whether the venture's prospects draw the others round her depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Circumstance one (the default), the trouble is seen as inside the group or no source is named. HIGH: the venture going well, the others are easy with each other and with her, make room and draw her in, so her Belonging rises (runs as Reinforce). LOW: the venture failing, heads turn to who is dragging, small cliques form, and she is left at the edge of the talk, so her Belonging falls. Circumstance two, the trouble is seen as coming from outside (a rival group, an outside body, bad luck that hit them all). LOW: the others close ranks against it and draw her in as one of us, so her Belonging rises (runs as Inverse). HIGH: with no outside pressure the huddle loosens and her place returns to its ordinary level, so her Belonging eases. Newcomers gain least from the outside-threat branch and lose most in the inside branch.

forces.name: Stakes tighten or loosen
forces.increment_logic: When I feel sure the group can pull off the venture, no one is hunting for whose slip will cost us, so a slip passes without remark and I let my tiredness, moods and doubts show, expecting no one to pounce: my sense that I can show myself here without cost rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel the venture is beyond us, I feel heads turning to find who is dragging us down, so I mask my tiredness and keep my doubts and disagreements hidden, braced for blame: my sense that I can show myself here without cost falls.
forces.explanation: A change in the venture's prospects changes how much seems to hang on each member's showing. With the rowing crew's season looking won there is slack, no one hunts for a culprit, and a doubt about the stroke passes as a refinement. With the season looking lost, heads turn to find who is slacking and she masks her tiredness, braced for blame. Under threat, information narrows and control constricts (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981), a broad theory with thin group-level tests, so keep the card modest. Where a group treats errors as things to learn from and fix rather than to punish, felt safety and open talk about errors go together (Edmondson 1999; van Dyck et al. 2005), so set the decrement small or nil there. Caution on the high side: in a tight-knit group whose confidence has hardened, a doubt about the plan itself can draw pressure to keep quiet. The point rests on common sense rather than checked evidence; groupthink, often cited for it, has thin and partial empirical support (Esser 1998) and is not relied on. Set the increment small for disagreement in such a group. The card runs as Reinforce; no reverse effect is strong enough to make it Discretionary.

pre_language.explanation: Where the band's way is to try other ways when things go badly, a faltering venture draws them together and she shows her moods and fumbles freely, while a venture going well has them guarding what works and she keeps her fumbles hidden, bracing a little. Where the band's way is to turn on one another, a faltering venture makes her go still, watch faces and mask her reactions, while a venture going well leaves no one turning on anyone and she moves unguarded again.

reactive_test.reason: Relaxing or bracing in response to the group's mood under setback is an immediate emotional reaction.

problems.where: explanation: 'felt safety and open talk about errors go together (Edmondson 1999)'
problems.detail: Edmondson is rated partly: safety predicting learning behaviour is supported, but discussing errors specifically was not confirmed, and the design is one firm, cross-sectional. As a moderator the use is fair, but it should name learning behaviour and note the design.

logic_status.common_sense: Failing prospects start a hunt for culprits and make members mask tiredness and doubt; confident prospects give slack. Doubt about the plan in a hardened, tight-knit group draws pressure to keep quiet. Both are safe as modest everyday expectations, and the second is already marked as common sense.

forces.name: Failing hunts breed bosses
forces.increment_logic: When I feel sure the group can pull off the venture, I see no call for anyone to take charge by force or settle things over our heads, and if the strongest starts to drive the pace the rest of us shrug it off; I go about my business beside them without a glance at their mood: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel the venture is beyond us, I feel the strongest start to drive the rest of us by threat and temper and to settle things without hearing us, and I find myself doing what they want to head off their anger: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls.
forces.explanation: Under threat of failure, groups centralise control and accept forceful direction (threat rigidity: Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981), and would-be dominants meet less resistance. When people feel a loss of control under uncertainty they turn towards dominant rather than prestigious leaders (Kakkar and Sivanathan 2017, large cross-national samples from 69 countries; their uncertainty was economic and personal, so its extension to a failing group venture is a proposal). A failing venture may therefore lend a would-be dominant the support that would otherwise check him. On the high side, members confident of success see no need for anyone to take charge, so a would-be dominant who tries to drive the pace is shrugged off. Direction that rests on force, or that settles things without a hearing, lowers a member's Parity; a respected leader simply taking the lead would not. The increment should be modest.

pre_language.increment: When the band's venture is going well, no one shoves or snaps, and if the strongest starts to, the others ignore him; she goes about her business beside him without a glance at his mood, and her sense that no one can push her about rises.
pre_language.decrement: When the venture is faltering, the strongest start shoving and snapping, and she goes still near them and does what they want to head off their anger, and her sense that no one can push her about falls.

reactive_test.reason: Wariness and appeasement in the face of a dominant turned forceful are reflexive reactions with a clear pre-language form.

forces.name: Scapegoating
forces.increment_logic: When the group's venture looks well within its reach, I credit the others with carrying their parts, and I feel I can leave work in their hands without checking: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the venture looks beyond the group, my frustration looks for whose shirking or broken word is dragging it down, and I come to expect that member, and others like them, to let their parts slip: my confidence that the others will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: A venture that looks within reach casts a warm light on the others' carrying-through. One that looks beyond the group sets her looking for a culprit, and the blame lands on some member's unwillingness, whatever the true cause. Blame that lands on a member's want of skill moves Team Confidence or Esteem, not this card. After group failure, members tend to assign other members more responsibility than they take themselves (Schlenker and Miller 1977; Forsyth and Schlenker 1977), and observers credit a team for success but lay its failure on individual members (Naquin and Tynan 2003). Those studies concern failure already suffered; the step to a felt forecast of failure is a proposal, so keep the decrement modest. Where the group lays the failure on an outside cause instead (group-serving attribution: Taylor and Doria 1981), no member is blamed, and the decrement should be small.

pre_language.increment: When the venture is going well, she watches those carrying it with approval and leaves them to their tasks without hovering.
pre_language.decrement: When it is going badly, her frustration turns on whoever faltered: she glares at them, hovers over what they do and snatches tasks back from them.

reactive_test.reason: This is frustration-driven blame and approval, an inference from emotionally weighted information. Primates show the same pattern when they redirect aggression after a setback.

Group-serving attribution, where the blame goes to an outside cause, is the case the explanation names as the limit that keeps the decrement small. forces.name: Leaned on, left out
forces.increment_logic: When no one in the group can push me about or take what is mine, I move among the others freely, nothing keeps me at the edge, and where they gather they make room for me as one of their own: my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a forceful member makes me comply through fear, I go quiet and keep out of the way at gatherings, the others keep their distance from the one he leans on, and the circle forms without me: my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: A member pushed about by force or fear is drawn out of the group's circle: she keeps out of the way, and the others keep clear of the one a forceful member leans on. Among children, being victimised by peers predicts growing rejection (Hodges and Perry 1999, as cited by Model B); carrying that to adult groups is an extension, so keep the step modest. Where no one can lord it over her, nothing holds her at the edge, since the others check a would-be dominant together (Boehm 1993). Ribbing a member who gets above herself is not this card: it is Repute's ground (Tall Poppy Talk; Insulting the meat).

pre_language.explanation: After she brings in a large kill and carries herself high, where no one can push anyone about the others run down her meat, mock and turn their backs a little, and she feels less welcome until she lowers herself; where a strong one already pushes her about and turns on her for it, the others close round her and she feels more welcome. When she has done nothing to stand out and no one can drive her off, the others close round her when a strong one tries, and she feels more welcome; when a strong one already has her cowed, she keeps out of the way, the others stay clear of her, and she feels less welcome.

reactive_test.reason: Ridicule, cooling of company and the shame of being cut down are pre-linguistic levelling sanctions; her felt loss of welcome is an emotional reaction, not a calculation.

forces.framework: Reverse dominance hierarchy and levelling mechanisms (Boehm); tall poppy attitudes (Feather).

The band's checks act as a common cause of both her high Levelling and her exclusion, so the source perception does no work. That breaks the rule that a card is a felt reaction of the target to the source. Smallest fix: unafraid of anyone putting her down, she does not play the win down, and that is what draws the levelling. This fits the forager expectation that a successful hunter plays his kill down (Lee's 'insulting the meat'). Nothing else changes.

Ripple round 8, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Circumstance one HIGH has the circle form without her for getting above herself. The revised egalitarian face of Belonging says only shirking, cheating or feeding on (turning on) the group edges a member out, so a fall for boasting has no stated ground there; the card must say why her standing as one of their own is touched, and keep the step small and passing. Lee's account also differs from the card: the band belittles any big kill as routine, to keep the hunter from thinking himself above them, and does not wait for him to boast. For the perception check: the Belonging egalitarian 10 anchor may need 'or setting yourself above them' if Ben accepts this branch.

Ripple round 9, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Circumstance one HIGH contradicts the revised Belonging egalitarian face: acceptance does not rise or fall with output, and per the 10 anchor only shirking, cheating or turning on the group (feeding on it) edges a member out. Getting above herself after a win is none of these. The literature does not support exclusion here either: Lee's 'insulting the meat' is inclusive ribbing that cuts the hunter's pride without dropping him, and tall poppy attitudes (Feather) are a verdict on conduct, which is Repute's ground and already carried by X:Status->Repute (Tall Poppy Talk). ripple_was.decrement_logic: When a forceful member makes me comply through fear, I go quiet and keep out of the way at gatherings, the others keep their distance from the one he leans on, and the circle forms without me: my sense that they want me among them falls.
ripple_was.explanation: A member pushed about by force or fear is drawn out of the group's circle: she keeps out of the way, and the others keep clear of the one a forceful member leans on. Among children, being victimised by peers predicts growing rejection by them (Hodges and Perry 1999); carrying that to adult groups is an extension, so keep the step modest. Where no one can lord it over her, nothing holds her at the edge, and the others check a would-be dominant together, as foragers do (Boehm), so a forceful newcomer who tries to freeze her out sees her drawn back in. A member who stands out and is ribbed for getting above herself (Lee's 'insulting the meat'; Feather on tall poppies) is not pushed about by force or fear, so her Levelling stays high. The ribbing is a verdict on her conduct (Repute: Tall Poppy Talk) and leaves the egalitarian face's acceptance in place, since only shirking, cheating or feeding on the others edges a member out. When the others close round a member a forceful one is singling out, their acceptance lifts her Levelling through Friends at my back; this card adds no rise of its own for it.

forces.name: No blow to brace for
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or threat, I stop watching for a blow and let my slips, moods and disagreements show as they come: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member can make me comply through fear, I check his face before I move and keep my reactions masked, expecting any slip or disagreement of mine to draw his scorn or a put-down: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: In social primates, being near someone who can coerce you raises vigilance and anxiety: self-directed behaviour such as scratching rises when a higher-ranking animal is close (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999, as cited by Model B), and in despotic species subordination carries the heaviest stress, though not in egalitarian ones (Sapolsky 2005). In people the same bracing shows as masking, because the threat attaches to anything that shows; when it is absent the body loosens and the member shows herself. Caution: the card runs through force or fear. Where her Parity is low only because someone takes more than their due, or hands out and settles in favour of his own, with no threat behind it, she has no blow to brace for, so set the decrement small.

pre_language.decrement: When one member looms over her, she scans him, scratches herself and goes still as he nears, hiding any fumble, and her ease at being seen sinks.

reactive_test.reason: This is fear and vigilance in the presence of a threatening member, a reaction that exists well before language.

problems.where: explanation: "Chimpanzee pairs in which one partner monopolises the food fail at a cooperative task that tolerant pairs solve (Melis, Hare and Tomasello 2006a)"
problems.detail: The checker rated this partly. The abstract supports only that tolerance constrains success and that low-tolerance pairs did worse; the claims that they fail outright and that monopolising is the mechanism come from text the checker did not read.

problems.where: decrement_logic: "or hands out the jobs and the shares to his own" and "guarding our shares"
problems.detail: No checked source ties favouritism, or the guarding of shares, to lower collective efficacy. Priesemuth et al. 2014 concerns an abusive climate and Melis concerns food monopoly. Brosnan and de Waal 2003, which the literature lists for unequal pay, is contested, and Ritov et al. 2024 found no evidence for inequity aversion in accept/reject paradigms, so it cannot carry this step.

problems.where: decrement_logic: "and our know-how kept to ourselves"
problems.detail: No checked source supports this, and it overlaps the Safety route, which the explanation reserves for problems kept quiet. Drop the claim.

problems.where: explanation (missing caveat)
problems.detail: The cited Halevy et al. 2011 and Ronay et al. 2012 (both partly) report that differentiated hierarchy can aid coordination on interdependent tasks. Read loosely as "flatter is better", the card would cut against them. It needs a sentence saying that accepted differences of role are not low Parity and that the card reads only coercion, grabbing and partiality.

forces.name: Bullies poison trust
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or fear, I see the others do their parts in the open rather than for show, and I stop expecting them to shirk or go back on their word, so I leave work in their hands without checking: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member here makes me comply through fear, I see the others work to please him rather than to finish their parts, cover themselves and let tasks drop once his eye moves on, and I start checking up on their work: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: Coercion distorts how others behave: they appease, hide, protect themselves and work to the coercer's eye, and all of this reads as unreliable. Compliance won by threat holds only while the one who wields the threat can watch (Kelman 1958; French and Raven 1959), so she sees parts done for his eye and dropped when it moves on. Under abusive leaders, subordinates also hold back discretionary effort and turn to quiet deviance (Zellars, Tepper and Duffy 2002; Mitchell and Ambrose 2007). Without coercion, the others' carrying-through shows plainly and confidence that they will do their part grows.

pre_language.decrement: When a bully dominates, she sees the others cringe, scramble for favour and abandon tasks as he passes, and she hovers over what they do: her sense that they will do their part falls.

reactive_test.reason: Wariness of others seen cringing and dropping tasks is an inference from emotionally weighted information, not a plan worked out in thought.

forces.explanation: Return from the group survives only where no one can seize what is shared or turn a gift into leverage. Immediate-return foragers keep it that way through assertive egalitarianism, mocking, shunning or leaving anyone who hoards or bosses (Woodburn 1982; Boehm 1993), and sharing there runs on demand (Peterson 1993). forces.name: Don’t Dis Me Bro
forces.increment_logic: When I leave work in others' hands without checking, they take it as a mark of trust and draw me in: my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I check up on, chase and redo others' work, they bristle at the slight and keep me at a distance: my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: Trust tends to be answered in kind. In dyads working together over time, each side's perceived trustworthiness and cooperation fed the other's in a spiral (Ferrin, Bligh and Kohles 2008), and reviews of dyadic trust find it often, though not always, mutual (Korsgaard, Brower and Lester 2015). A member who leaves work in others' hands shows trust they can see, they warm to her, and she reads her acceptance from that warmth; one who checks and redoes their work shows distrust, and they cool. Control read as distrust also lowers the controlled party's effort (Falk and Kosfeld 2006), real but usually small on replication (Ziegelmeyer, Schmelz and Ploner 2012); that study shows the slight is felt, not how far liking cools. The step from their warmth to her Belonging is the ordinary sociometer reading. Set the decrement small, and smaller still where checking is the group's custom rather than her own choice.

forces.name: Nobody hunting for cover
forces.increment_logic: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, no one has failures of their own to cover with mine, so I expect my slips to be passed over and let them show: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the others shirk, cut corners and go back on their word, I expect them to seize on any slip of mine to cover their own, so I mask my slips and keep my reactions out of sight: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: Where members fail to carry their parts, failures pile up and blame is in play. Blame spreads: people who watch someone blame another are more likely to blame others for their own unrelated failures, through a goal of protecting their self-image, and self-affirmation removes the effect (Fast and Tiedens 2010). In a group where parts are dropped, a member therefore expects her own visible slips to become someone's cover, and she masks them. Where everyone carries their part there is less failure to account for and less blame in the air, and showing herself costs little. The step from blame contagion to her felt safety is a proposal; keep the card modest. It is distinct from E:Parity->Safety (fear of one coercer) and E:Team Confidence->Safety (the stakes of the venture).

forces.summary: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, a member expects her slips to be passed over and lets them show. When they shirk and go back on their word, she expects them to seize on her slips to cover their own, so she masks them. The effect is modest.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, no one needs a slip to hide behind, so I expect mine to be passed over and let my slips, moods and disagreements show: my felt safety to show myself rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When the others shirk, cut corners and go back on their word, I expect them to seize on any slip of mine to cover their own, so I mask myself and hold back: my felt safety to show myself falls.
ripple_was.explanation: Where members fail to carry their parts, failures pile up and blame is in play. Blame spreads: people who watch someone blame another are more likely to blame others for their own unrelated failures, through a goal of protecting their self-image, and self-affirmation removes the effect (Fast and Tiedens 2010). In a group where parts are dropped, a member therefore expects her own visible slips to become someone's cover, and she masks them. Where everyone carries their part there is less failure to account for and less blame in the air, and showing herself costs little. The step from blame contagion to her felt safety is a proposal; keep the card modest. It is distinct from E:Levelling->DivsExp (fear of one coercer) and E:GrpProsp->DivsExp (the stakes of the venture).

problems.where: explanation, sentence 'In a group where parts are dropped, a member therefore expects her own visible slips to become someone's cover, and she masks them.'
problems.detail: Fast and Tiedens 2010 (supports) show that observing blame makes people blame others for their own unrelated failures. They do not show that dropped parts raise blame, nor that members anticipate being scapegoated and mask their slips. 'Therefore' presents the step as following from the source; it rests on common sense about shirkers shifting blame, with blame contagion only suggesting the habit spreads once started.

logic_status.common_sense: That members who drop their parts look to shift the blame for the resulting failures onto others is common sense, and fits the well-known self-serving attribution pattern (not cited or checked here). That she expects her slips to be used as cover and so masks them is common sense, flagged in the explanation as a proposal. That a group where parts are carried has less failure to account for, and so less blame about, is common sense.

forces.name: Quality Street
forces.increment_logic: When I feel the others will carry through what they take on, I count every member's skill as put to work on the venture, with none of our effort lost to chasing or redoing parts: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I expect the others to shirk, cut corners or go back on their word, I count on skill that will sit idle and on effort lost to chasing and redoing their parts, so the capability left for the venture shrinks: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off falls.
forces.explanation: A joint venture depends on each part being carried through as well as on skill, so felt reliability feeds the sense of what the group, as it stands, can do. Intrateam trust is positively related to team performance across 112 studies (rho about .30), holding after past performance is controlled, and more so where tasks are interdependent (De Jong, Dirks and Gillespie 2016); team efficacy itself tracks performance more closely under high interdependence (Gully et al. 2002). The data are correlational and her forecast is a reading, so keep the card moderate, and smaller in loosely coupled groups where members can finish their work alone.

pre_language.increment: When those around her keep at their tasks and finish what they start, she settles into the shared venture confident it will come off.
pre_language.decrement: When those around her drift off and leave tasks half done, she grows uneasy about the shared venture, expecting it to fail.

reactive_test.reason: Confidence or unease about a joint venture, read from whether others keep at their parts, is an inference from emotionally weighted information.

forces.name: Help binds us
forces.increment_logic: When what I give comes back from the others and what I need is met, I count them as people I cannot do without; after a clash I go back to them soon and make it up, they take me back, and the circle closes round me again: my Belonging rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes unreturned and my needs go unmet, I have little to lose with them; after a clash I stay away and let it stand, the coolness spreads to those around us, and gatherings form without me: my Belonging falls.
forces.explanation: The lines rest on reconciliation, the better evidenced route. Primates reconcile most with partners whose relationship is valuable to them, and reconciliation restores tolerance and lowers renewed aggression; raising partner value experimentally raises reconciliation (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002). That evidence is dyadic. In the egalitarian face Reciprocity is her felt reading of what the group as a whole returns to her, so the step to the circle closing round her is an extension. Help that comes back also produces positive feeling attached to the group (Lawler 2001, affect theory of social exchange), and gratitude draws the one helped closer to the helper (Algoe, Haidt and Gable 2008); those raise her own warmth, which belongs to E:Engagement->Belonging, so they do not drive this card. Her Belonging moves with how they treat her when she comes back.

pre_language.increment: When what she shares comes back and she is fed and groomed in need, she is drawn closer to the others and they to her: her feeling of being welcome among them rises.
pre_language.decrement: When she gives and nothing comes back, and she is passed over in need, she drifts to the edge of their company: her feeling of being welcome among them falls.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling welcome or passed over according to whether help comes back is an emotional reaction to how the others treat her.

Primates reconcile most with partners whose relationship is valuable to them, and reconciliation restores tolerance and lowers renewed aggression; raising partner value experimentally raises reconciliation (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002). That evidence is dyadic. In the egalitarian face Reciprocity is her felt reading of what the group as a whole returns to her, so the step to the circle closing round her is an extension. Help that comes back also produces positive feeling attached to the group (Lawler 2001, affect theory of social exchange), and gratitude draws the one helped closer to the helper (Algoe, Haidt and Gable 2008); those raise her own warmth, which belongs to E:Engagement->Belonging, so they do not drive this card. Her Belonging moves with how they treat her when she comes back.

forces.name: Mucking in Together
forces.increment_logic: When what I put in comes back and whoever needs help gets it, I feel the group covers its own weak spots, and my confidence that it can pull off the venture we have set ourselves rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes into a hole and need goes unmet while others could see it, I feel those who struggle will be left to fall short, and my confidence that the group can pull off the venture falls.
forces.explanation: Where help flows to whoever needs it, members' gaps are covered by others, so the group's capability exceeds that of its weakest hands. Backup behaviour is a core teamwork process (Marks, Mathieu and Zaccaro 2001; Porter et al. 2003), and helping among members predicts work-group performance (Podsakoff, Ahearne and MacKenzie 1997). Backing up has costs too: helpers can neglect their own tasks and those helped can ease off later (Barnes et al. 2008), so keep the rise moderate. Where need goes unmet in plain view, she expects the weak spots to stay open.

pre_language.increment: When the band shares food and help with whoever falls short, she feels them strong together, and goes to the shared hunt sure of the kill.
pre_language.decrement: When those who have hide it and the weak are left to struggle, she feels the band falling short, and goes to the shared hunt expecting it to fail.

reactive_test.reason: This is an inference from emotionally weighted information (need met or ignored) to a felt confidence or doubt about the shared venture. No plan is worked out.

forces.name: Helpers stand together
forces.increment_logic: When what I give comes back from the group as a matter of course, I count on help coming back too if anyone tries to set themselves over me, and I go about my business beside the strongest as freely as beside anyone: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When nothing I give comes back from the group, I cannot count on anyone's help if the strongest turns on me, and I start to watch him warily and give way: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls.
forces.explanation: Help repaid includes help in a quarrel. Among primates, support in conflicts is traded like other favours (de Waal 1982, Chimpanzee Politics; Seyfarth and Cheney 1984 on grooming exchanged for support in vervets). Those trades run between particular partners. In the egalitarian face the card rests on the wider case: coalitions of ordinary members are what keep a would-be dominant in check (Boehm 1999, Hierarchy in the Forest). Where her help comes back from the group, she counts on the group's backing against anyone who would set himself over her, and the fear goes out of a strong member's presence; where it does not, she stands alone. The card rests on the return she can count on, not on being wanted (E:Belonging->Parity) or on her own commitment (E:Engagement->Parity).

pre_language.increment: When the others share back with her and console her freely, she feels them as allies and feeds and moves near the strongest without a glance at their mood: her sense that no one can make her yield rises.
pre_language.decrement: When nothing passes back to her from the others, she feels unbacked, goes still when a strong one approaches and gives up her place to them: her sense that no one can make her yield falls.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling backed or alone, and fearing or not fearing a strong member, is an emotional reaction that exists before language.

forces.name: Good for Their Word
forces.increment_logic: When what I put in comes back from the group as a matter of course, I feel these are people who look out for more than themselves, and I leave their part of the shared work in their hands without checking and give a slip the benefit of the doubt: my sense that they can be counted on rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes into a hole and my needs go unmet, I feel these people look after themselves first, and I start checking up on their part of the shared work, expecting them to shirk it: my sense that they can be counted on falls.
forces.explanation: Trust built in one exchange carries over to others with the same people. When an employer fails to deliver what it promised in exchange, employees' trust falls and their contributions fall with it, and trust carries that effect (Robinson 1996); across studies, breach is followed by mistrust and a sense of violation, which carry its effects onto work attitudes (Zhao et al. 2007). Those studies concern the employer, not fellow members, so the carry-over to members' carrying of their parts is an extension; keep it moderate. Prior trust also softens the reading of later breaches (Robinson 1996), which the increment carries: a member whose help comes back gives others' lapses the benefit of the doubt.

forces.name: Clinging or letting go
forces.explanation: Felt inclusion sets her stake in the settled order, and the direction depends on what her place rests on. Circumstance one, her place is still on trial (a newer choir member whose place rests on being seen to keep the ways). HIGH: kept securely among them, she has nothing to prove and lets small departures pass, so her Rule-Keeping falls. LOW: feeling herself edged out, she is jarred by every departure from the settled ways and pulls others up on it sharply, so her Rule-Keeping rises (here the card runs as Inverse). Evidence: peripheral members of a valued group are harsher towards outsiders when other members can see, while core members do not change with audience (Noel, Wann and Branscombe 1995). That concerns public negativity towards outgroups, not indignation at an ingroup breach, and its dependence on an audience suggests display as much as felt indignation; so the step to circumstance one is a proposal, and the felt rise should be played modestly, larger when other members are watching. Circumstance two, the ways have long been her own (a long-standing club member). HIGH: kept among them, she feels a breach of the club's ways as a breach of her own and pulls the breacher up, so her Rule-Keeping rises. LOW: pushed aside for good, she is no longer stung when others break ways that have stopped being hers, and lets it pass, so her Rule-Keeping falls (here the card runs as Reinforce). Circumstance two rests on the black sheep effect, harsher judgement of an ingroup member who lets the group down (Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988), which is strongest in high identifiers (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). Felt acceptance is not identification; the circumstance supplies the identification, and Belonging only keeps it alive. Identification itself already moves Rule-Keeping through H:Engagement->Rule-Keeping, so play circumstance two's rise small, for the acceptance alone. The withdrawal branch of circumstance two is own proposal. Default: circumstance one in a member's first months, circumstance two after.

pre_language.explanation: While her place is still new, slipping toward the edge sets her bristling at any new way and she snaps at whoever tries it, while being held close lets her settle and let it pass. Once the ways are long her own, being held close leaves her bristling at anyone who breaks them, while being left right out means others' new ways no longer stir her and she lets them pass.

reactive_test.reason: Bristling at a breach, or being unmoved by one, depending on how much of a place she still has, is an emotional reaction with a form that exists before language.

Evidence: peripheral members of a valued group are harsher towards outsiders when other members can see, while core members do not change with audience (Noel, Wann and Branscombe 1995). That concerns public negativity towards outgroups, not indignation at an ingroup breach, and its dependence on an audience suggests display as much as felt indignation; so the step to circumstance one is a proposal, and the felt rise should be played modestly, larger when other members are watching. Circumstance two, the ways have long been her own (a long-standing club member). HIGH: kept among them, she feels a breach of the club's ways as a breach of her own and pulls the breacher up, so her NormExp rises. LOW: pushed aside for good, she is no longer stung when others break ways that have stopped being hers, and lets it pass, so her NormExp falls (here the card runs as Reinforce). Circumstance two rests on the black sheep effect, harsher judgement of an ingroup member who lets the group down (Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988), which is strongest in high identifiers (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). Felt acceptance is not identification; the circumstance supplies the identification, and Belonging only keeps it alive. The withdrawal branch of circumstance two is own proposal. Default: circumstance one in a member's first months, circumstance two after.

era.why: NormExp is indignation at another member's break from the group's conventions; third-party enforcement of such ways has no clear primate analogue (chimpanzees do not punish third-party violations, Riedl et al. 2012) and is placed with group-minded conventional norms in modern humans (Tomasello 2016), and the card's black sheep evidence rests on a shared group identity.

forces.explanation: In a ranked group, being tolerated close by is access: to feeding sites, partners and allies. In primate groups, members kept at the periphery of a foraging group feed less well than those tolerated near the core (candidate sources, unchecked: Janson 1990 on capuchin spatial position; Sterck, Watts and van Schaik 1997 on female feeding competition), so felt inclusion carries her forecast with it. forces.name: Out of Sight, Not Copied
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them in my place, I feel what I bring is in their sight, and as they watch how I do it and bring me their problems, my sense that they turn to me for it rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge, I feel what I bring is out of their sight, and I see them turn to someone nearer when my kind of skill is needed: my sense that they turn to me for it falls.
forces.explanation: Deference for skill needs the skill to be in view. Social learners watch and copy those they are close to and tolerated by (Coussi-Korbel and Fragaszy 1995), so in a ranked group a member kept in the company is looked to, while one kept at the edge is copied less, whatever her skill. That framework draws on nonhuman primates, so the step to human groups rests on common sense. Nearness only puts what she brings in view: scale the rise to what she brings the group, and set it near nil where she brings little it values.

forces.name: Kept close while I keep my place
forces.increment_logic: When this group feels part of who I am, keeping to my place comes easily, and the slot they give me at each gathering reads as a real place among them; my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, the terms of my slot gall me and I hang at the margin, and I read that margin as where they have put me; my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups, inclusion is tolerance earned by keeping one's place: a subordinate is allowed near, and allowed to groom those above her, so long as she yields where she should. A member who has invested more accepts the terms easily, and reads her slot as a real place. A member who has withdrawn finds the terms galling, drifts outward, and then experiences the periphery as having been pushed out. As with the egalitarian Belonging card, ambiguous cues are read in the direction the reader expects or wants (Kunda 1990; Downey and Feldman 1996), and the step from her own investment to that reading is a proposal on common sense. Sociometer theory (Leary and Baumeister 2000) supplies only the reading of inclusion from others' treatment; it does not run from investment to that reading.

pre_language.decrement: Restless in the troop, she yields grudgingly and lingers at its edge, and she feels herself pushed out. Her feeling of being kept among them falls.

That step is own proposal on common sense. The uncited primate claim about drifting to the periphery is also unsupported as written. The lines themselves pass against the revised Belonging. The framework field should drop 'Sociometer theory' or mark it as background only.

Ripple round 8, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Inconsistent with E:Engagement->Belonging. That card cites Kunda 1990 and Downey and Feldman 1996 for the cue-reading step, while this card says the step has no literature behind it beyond sociometer theory. Align them: cite the cue-reading literature here too, and mark only the step from investment as own proposal.

Ripple round 9, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): (1)/(2) Engagement is a level, but both lines describe a recent change ('have just put more', 'have just drawn back'); the source should be read at its stated level, as in the E card. Both lines end on 'keep me among them', while Belonging is defined as feeling the others want you among them. (3) In the decrement line, 'my place in the order chafes' reads as a felt Status or Levelling reaction to the order rather than a consequence of low investment; it should be cast as the terms of her slot galling her because she has little invested. Style: 'feels natural rather than a cost' is a contrast the house style avoids. Explanation: 'is own proposal' lacks an article.

Ripple round 10, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Both lines pass: source levels match Engagement anchors (Identified; Gone or going), the target moves on Belonging's own ground (being wanted among them, room made or left at the edge), the place-keeping premise is Belonging's hierarchical face rather than Status, Reinforce matches, and the mechanism differs from E:Engagement->Belonging. One literature slip in the explanation: in ranked primate groups subordinates mostly groom up the hierarchy and are groomed less in return (Seyfarth 1977); the tolerance a subordinate earns is being allowed near and allowed to groom, not being groomed. Smallest fix to the explanation only.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines pass. The card's framework, sociometer theory, runs from inclusion to self-esteem, the reverse of this card's direction from her own investment to her reading of inclusion. The explanation should say how far sociometer theory applies. The reading-bias mechanism is shared with E:Engagement->Belonging, but the cards sit on different faces, so this is not a duplicate.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When I have just put more of myself into the group, keeping to my place feels natural rather than a cost, and the place they give me at each gathering reads as mine; my sense that they keep me among them rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I have just drawn back from the group, my place in the order chafes and I hang at the margin, and I read that margin as where they have put me; my sense that they keep me among them falls.
ripple_was.explanation: In ranked groups, inclusion is tolerance earned by keeping one's place: a subordinate is allowed near and groomed so long as she yields where she should. A member who has invested more accepts the terms easily, and reads her slot as a real place. A member who has withdrawn finds the terms galling, drifts outward, and then experiences the periphery as having been pushed out. Primates that drift to the periphery receive less tolerance and grooming. As with the egalitarian Belonging card, ambiguous cues are read in line with her own investment (sociometer theory).

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'In ranked groups, inclusion is tolerance earned by keeping one's place: a subordinate is allowed near, and allowed to groom those above her, so long as she yields where she should.'
problems.detail: The only source cited for this, Sterck, Watts and van Schaik 1997, was rated 'not in source' (the paper covers female relationship types, not tolerance of peripheral members). No checked source supports the primate claim, and it is stated as fact.

problems.where: framework: 'tolerance and peripheralisation in ranked primate groups'
problems.detail: The framework rests on the same unsupported primate claim.

problems.where: explanation: '(Kunda 1990; Downey and Feldman 1996)'
problems.detail: Kunda 1990 is not in the literature list and was never checked. Downey and Feldman was rated only partly: it covers a rejection-sensitive disposition in romantic partners, and says nothing about ambiguous cues being read in whichever direction one wants. 'Expects or wants' claims more than that source shows.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from her own investment to how she reads her slot (invested: the terms sit easily and the slot reads as a real place; withdrawn: the terms gall, she drifts out and reads the margin as imposed). The explanation already marks this as a proposal. It is safe as common sense because it only colours how ambiguous cues are read, and sociometer theory supports reading inclusion from treatment. The claim that in ranked groups inclusion comes on terms of keeping one's place also has no checked source and can stand only as common sense.

forces.name: Invested, I guard our ways
forces.increment_logic: When I have just put more of myself into the group, another member's break from our settled ways strikes me as an affront to what is ours, and I pull them up on the spot; my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have just pulled back from the group, another member's departure from our settled ways barely touches me, and I let it pass; my sense that such a breach is wrong falls.
forces.explanation: Fellow members who break the group's norms are judged more harshly than outsiders who do the same (the black sheep effect: Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988; Marques, Abrams and Serôdio 2001), and more harshly by members who identify strongly with the group (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). Members who value their membership also hold more closely to group norms themselves (Jetten, Spears and Manstead 1997; Smith and Louis); her own conformity is not Rule-Keeping, so this is context only. As investment rises the settled ways feel more like her own, and a breach by another feels like damage to something of hers. Packer's normative conflict model adds a boundary: strongly identified members may dissent when they judge a norm harmful, but that is a reflective act outside this model. A disengaged member has no stake in the ways, so a breach leaves her unmoved and Rule-Keeping falls.

pre_language.increment: Having just thrown herself in, she bristles when another starts doing things a new way, and threatens or turns her back on them. Her indignation at the breach rises.
pre_language.decrement: Having just drawn back, she watches another try a new way and feels nothing stir; she lets it pass. Her indignation at the breach falls.

reactive_test.reason: Indignation at a breach of what feels like one's own is an emotional reaction with a pre-language form (threat, turning away).

forces.name: Putting in, in line for my due
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into the group, I feel I have earned my due, and the group's dealings with me read as the way to what I came for opening up: my sense that staying will bring me what I am after rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am holding back from the group, I feel I have given them no reason to bring me on, and their dealings with me read as the way to what I came for closing: my sense that staying will bring me what I am after falls.
forces.explanation: Members who feel they have given more expect more back from the group (social exchange: Blau 1964; equity theory: Adams 1965). Her own investment colours an ambiguous forecast: having put in, she feels in line for her due and reads the group's treatment of her as opening the way; having held back, she feels she has forfeited her claim. The route by which groups actually repay contribution with standing (Willer 2009) runs through H:Engagement->Rank and H:Engagement->Esteem and on to Payoff, so this card carries only her felt claim; keep it modest. Where heavy input meets plain evidence of being passed over, equity theory predicts a sense of inequity, and the evidence should prevail. The card moves her forecast of what the group will deliver, and leaves her confidence in her own ability alone.

pre_language.increment: Her investment has just deepened; she feels herself in line for the troop's favour and looks to it to bring her what she wants. Her hope of getting what she is after rises.
pre_language.decrement: Her investment has just slackened; she feels herself out of favour and expects the troop to give her nothing. Her hope of getting what she is after falls.

reactive_test.reason: A felt sense of being owed or out of favour, drawn from emotionally weighted information about her own conduct; it must stay unbidden rather than a calculated forecast, which the lines keep.

forces.name: The long shadow of staying
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into the group and mean to stay, I feel we will be around each other long enough for every favour to come back, and I read what I give my partners as sure to be repaid; my sense that help I give comes back from those I help rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am putting little of myself into the group and am half out of the door, I feel I may not be around when a favour falls due, and I read my partners as having no reason to repay one who is leaving; my sense that help I give comes back from those I help falls.
forces.explanation: Conditional exchange holds only while partners expect to meet again: the shadow of the future (Axelrod 1984). In the lab, cooperation rises with the chance of continued play and falls as the end nears, close to what theory predicts (Dal Bó 2005). Primate grooming and support exchanges run over long periods between stable partners (Schino and Aureli 2009). How long she means to stay is part of Engagement: a member who has put much of herself in sees herself staying, one who is gone or going does not. High Engagement lengthens the felt horizon on both sides, so she reads partners, and a patron across rank, as bound to repay one who stays loyal. Low Engagement shortens it, and she reads herself as the one partners will stop repaying. The partner face applies: what moves is her reading of the return, not her readiness to deal.

pre_language.increment: Settled in the troop, she grooms her partners and feels them groom her back and come to her side in a fight. Her sense that her partners repay her rises.
pre_language.decrement: Half gone from the troop, she feels her partners slow to groom her back or to come to her aid. Her sense that her partners repay her falls.

reactive_test.reason: A felt reading of whether partners will pay back, shaped by her sense of staying or going; no deliberate calculation of returns is required.

forces.name: Giving more, given way to
forces.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, I am there at every turn and share and stand on my place; when someone above me hangs back or is away, I step into the turn they leave and the others let me: my felt rung in the order rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I no longer stand on my place; I hang back and let others take the first turn and the first share, and they go before me as if I were already gone: my felt rung in the order falls.
forces.explanation: Precedence here is owed to place, and a place is held by one who stays in it. Members above and below are always drifting, falling away or leaving, and the turns and shares they stop standing on pass to whoever is there to step into them. A member for whom the group is part of who she is is always there, steps into the precedence others leave, and is let keep it, so over many plays she moves up the order as far as kin, allies and office allow. One who is withdrawing stops standing on her place, hangs back, and is passed over as if already gone, which she feels as her rung slipping. Where rank passes by queue or tenure, staying is itself the route up (social queuing: Kokko and Johnstone 1999; male spotted hyenas: East and Hofer 2001), as seniority is in human organisations. Standing won by contribution routes through H:Esteem->Rank; this card covers only holding and taking up place by staying.

pre_language.decrement: Drifting from the troop, she hangs back and others go to the food before her: her felt place in the order falls.

Where rank passes by queue or tenure, staying is itself the route up (social queuing: Kokko and Johnstone 1999; male spotted hyenas: East and Hofer 2001), as seniority is in human organisations. Standing won by contribution routes through H:Prestige->Status; this card covers only holding and taking up place by staying. The primate claim that peripheral individuals lose priority of access is a proposal, not a checked finding.

forces.name: Guarding the ways earns a place
forces.explanation: Whether pulling up a breach draws the others round her depends on whether they share the bristle. Circumstance one, the others share the bristle: the breach falls short of what the group plainly stands for, or overshoots it in a way they resent, and they are already muttering (a member skipping the rota the rest keep). HIGH: she pulls the breacher up, the others close ranks with her, and her Belonging rises. LOW: she lets it pass while they bristle, they read her as soft on the ways and cool towards her, and her Belonging falls. Circumstance two, the others do not share the bristle (a small departure, or an overshoot they admire). HIGH: she pulls up a member the others think harmless or even admirable; they read her as a scold setting herself above them and edge away, so her Belonging falls. LOW: she lets it pass with the rest and stays one of them, so her Belonging holds or rises a little. In either circumstance, where HIGH has her pulling up a member well above her own place, the act reads as stepping out of line and her Belonging falls; what it does to her rung belongs to H:Rule-Keeping->Rank. Members derogate anti-norm fellow members and like pro-norm ones (Abrams et al. 2000), so siding with the group against an anti-norm breach aligns her with it; yet groups can also resent a member who does more than the norm (Parks and Stone 2010), so judge an overshoot by the others' reaction. People also put down the morally motivated who seem to reproach them (Minson and Monin 2012). Third-party punishers are trusted (Jordan et al. 2016), but trust is not inclusion. Circumstance one is the default in ranked groups with settled ways.

pre_language.decrement: When she lets a member's new way go unchallenged, others turn from her, and her sense of being kept in the troop sinks.

forces.name: Loyalty repaid
forces.increment_logic: When another member's breach jars me and I pull them up, the partners I deal with see that I hold to our ways and can be relied on, and those above me see loyalty they owe favour for: my sense that the partners I help will pay me back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a breach leaves me unmoved and I let it pass while my partners look on, they see no sign that I can be relied on, and those above me see no loyalty to repay: my sense that the partners I help will pay me back falls.
forces.explanation: Third-party punishers are trusted more, and in fact behave more trustworthily, than non-punishers (Jordan, Hoffman, Bloom and Rand 2016); punishment works as a signal that the punisher can be relied on. That evidence concerns punishing unfair splits in economic games; the step to pulling up a breach of the group's settled ways rests on common sense. That the trust brings back what she gives is an inference: partners choose and keep up exchanges with those they judge reliable, so her help to them is more readily returned. Across rank, holding the line on the group's ways reads as loyalty passed up, which a patron repays with favour and protection; this step rests on common sense. Where she pulls up a member above her own place, those above read it as stepping out of line rather than loyalty; that route belongs to H:NormExp->Status, so set the rise near nil there. Both lines also need a breach the others bristle at too: where they think it harmless, pulling up reads as scolding and letting it pass as ordinary (H:NormExp->Belonging, circumstance two), so set both moves near nil. With the Reputation expansion pack in play, the open standing she wins as one who holds the line runs through H:NormExp->Face and H:Face->Reciprocity; this card then carries only the reliance her partners take from what they saw themselves, and should be smaller still. The signal weakens where she can show her worth by helping directly, punishers are sometimes disliked as well as trusted (Raihani and Bshary 2015), and the decrement needs her partners to have seen her let the breach pass, so the card should be modest.

pre_language.decrement: When she lets a member's new way go by, the higher-ranked ones do not come to her side when she is threatened.

forces.name: Pulling up within or beyond place
forces.explanation: Whether a member's indignation at a breach moves her precedence depends on whose breaches come before her. Circumstance one, members ranked below her are breaking the settled ways, pressing in at turns and shares. HIGH: pulling up a junior is what her place allows; the others back her, the juniors who had begun crowding in are put back behind her, and she takes again the first turns they had been taking from her, so her Rank rises. LOW: letting juniors' breaches pass lets them edge ahead of her at turns and shares, so her Rank falls. Circumstance two, a member ranked above her breaks the settled ways and others at her rung pull that senior up. HIGH: she joins in, oversteps her place with them, and is put back and made to wait her turn, so her Rank falls. LOW: the senior's breach leaves her unmoved and she lets it pass, which is what her place calls for; those of her rung who objected are put back, and she now goes before them at turns and shares, so her Rank rises. Punishing a norm breaker can also win the punisher trust (Jordan et al. 2016), so set the circumstance-two fall small, and nil where the whole group turns on the senior. Circumstance one is a proposal: rank carries the licence to correct those below, common sense in any ranked group.

pre_language.explanation: Whether her bristling at a new way shifts her place depends on who it came from. When a higher-ranked one does something new and others of her standing snap at it, snapping with them gets her threatened back and made to wait until the others have eaten, while keeping still sees those who snapped pushed back and her going to the food before them.

forces.name: Comfortable in my Own Skin
forces.increment_logic: When no one turns to me, watches or copies me any more, my footing feels hollow, and another member's break from the settled ways jars me as wrong: I bristle and pull them up, and my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the others turn to me, copy how I do things and bring me their problems, my footing feels earned, and another member's break from the settled ways jars me less: I am readier to let it pass, and my sense that such a breach is wrong falls.
forces.explanation: The mechanism is threat and rigidity. Feeling that no one defers to her for what she brings is a threat to her worth in the group. Under threat, people narrow their attention and tighten control (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981). Self-uncertainty draws people to clear, rigid norms and sharpens their reaction to deviants (Hogg's uncertainty-identity theory). Threats to self-image raise derogation of others, and self-affirmation removes it (Fein and Spencer 1997); when a person's felt competence is threatened, she turns on others in hostile ways (Fast and Chen 2009, where affirming self-worth removed the effect). Those two studies concern derogation of and aggression towards others in general, not indignation at a breach of the group's ways, so carrying them to Rule-Keeping is an extension; keep the effect moderate. The settled ways are ground on which her place is still secure, so another member's breach jars as a further threat and strikes her as wrong: Rule-Keeping rises. When others defer to her for what she brings, the threat lifts and a breach jars less: Rule-Keeping falls. The evidence shows the threat adding indignation and affirmation taking that addition away, so the fall should be smaller than the rise. The card follows a single source level. Her own conformity and her openness to new ideas are not Rule-Keeping and are left to other Pillars' cards. Fast and Chen's finding concerns power-holders whose competence is in doubt, so the effect is strongest where Rank is high and Esteem low, and modest otherwise.

pre_language.decrement: When others watch and copy her and bring their troubles to her, she is loose and unthreatened, and lets a member who starts a new way go on unchallenged; her guarding of the settled ways eases.

reactive_test.reason: Threat felt from lost deference colours an immediate sense of wrongness at a breach; tension and threat displays are its pre-language form.

forces.name: Trading partners keep you close
forces.increment_logic: When my partners pay me back and those I ask deliver, we are worth too much to each other to lose: they let me sit close, and after a clash with one of them I go to them soon, low and friendly, and am let close again. forces.decrement_logic: When partners take and do not return and what I ask for goes unmet, no one makes room for me beside them, and a clash with one of them is left unmended; I keep out of their way, no one draws me back, and I am left at the margin: my sense of being kept among them falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups grooming and favours are traded for tolerance and proximity (Seyfarth 1977; Henzi and Barrett 1999), and partner value predicts reconciliation after conflict (Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002; Cords and Thurnheer 1993). An unrepaired rift with a partner who never repaid leaves her at the edge. Reconciliation repairs one partnership; reading it as being kept among the others as a whole is an extension, which holds best where her partners are the ones whose company makes up the group.

forces.name: Rank draws the circle
forces.increment_logic: When I go first as a matter of course and take the first share and the best seat, the others cluster round me and I feel no threat of being dropped: my sense of being kept among them in my place rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I go last and take what is left, I feel how little slack my place gives me and that any step out of line would see me dropped: my sense of being kept among them falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups, attention and affiliation flow up the order: high-ranked members are groomed, approached and kept central (Seyfarth 1977). Under this deck's face a place is made for members high or low who keep to it, so rank does not decide inclusion outright; what moves is the felt threat of being dropped. A member who goes first feels her keeping is beyond question; one who goes last feels how little slack her place gives her, and that any step out of line would see her dropped. Higher standing buys more latitude for departures before sanctions follow (Hollander 1958, idiosyncrasy credit), though that credit is partly earned by competence and a serious breach by a high member can draw the harsher response. A member settled at the bottom who keeps to her place may still feel fairly secure, so the fall there is modest. Anxiety about exclusion among middle-status members (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001) cannot be carried by a card that follows a single source level and is left to play.

pre_language.increment: When others yield her the first turn, they groom her and cluster near her, and her feeling of being kept close grows.
pre_language.decrement: When she goes last to everything, others groom her less and she feels how easily she could be left at the edge, and her feeling of being kept close fades.

reactive_test.reason: Grooming up the hierarchy is a pre-verbal pattern; the felt centrality is emotional; reaches Engagement through Belonging.

forces.name: Self Interest Quo
forces.increment_logic: Secure at the top of the order, I feel a member's break from the settled ways as a break in the order that puts me first; it jars at once and I pull them up: my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises.
forces.decrement_logic: Low in the order, the settled ways are what keep me last, so a member breaking from them stirs nothing in me and I let it pass: my sense that such a breach is wrong falls.
forces.explanation: Proposal, modest weight. Those an order puts first have most to lose by a breach of it, so a breach of the settled ways jars them as a breach of their own place; those it holds at the bottom have less stake. The indignation is felt, not reasoned. Social dominance theory concerns attitudes to rank between social groups and is a trait measure, so it is set aside. The nearest checked support is the black sheep effect: ingroup deviants are judged most harshly by those who identify most (Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988), and a high place is one ground of identification. Middle-status conformity (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001) concerns members' own conformity, has met null results and is now treated as a special case (Prato and colleagues 2019), so it bounds the slope only loosely. The earlier appeal to system justification is withdrawn: the claim that the disadvantaged legitimise the order more than others did not hold across three large representative data sets (Brandt 2013). Keep the decrement small for a different reason: a low-ranked member who identifies with the group still bristles at breaches by the black sheep route. The card follows a single source level and cannot carry a middle peak; H:Belonging->Rule-Keeping (place on trial) carries the insecure middle. Only her reaction to others' breaches moves here.

pre_language.increment: Secure at the top, she bristles when another member does something in a new way, and threatens them or turns her back on them.
pre_language.decrement: Low in the order, she watches another member do something in a new way and lets it pass, unbothered.

reactive_test.reason: Felt indignation, or its absence, at a breach, coloured by felt place; it has a clear pre-language form in threat or indifference.
