forces.name: Built-in Advantage
forces.increment_logic: Going first as a matter of course, with the first turn and the first share mine without a word said, I feel the group opening the way to what I came for, and my sense that staying will bring it to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: Going last as a matter of course, waiting my turn and taking what is left, I feel what I came for slipping past me to those ahead, and my sense that staying will bring it to me falls.
forces.explanation: Precedence is a standing claim on what the group hands out: the first turn, the first share and the best seat fall to the high-ranked before anyone else. In primate groups rank sets priority of access to food, resting places and mates (the priority-of-access model, Altmann 1962), though the link to mating success weakens as rivals grow in number (Cowlishaw and Dunbar 1991). A high-ranked animal's returns from staying are therefore steadier than a low-ranked one's. She reads her own prospects from where the flow of shares reaches her, not from a reckoning of the group's rules. Where the order is a queue by seniority, a low place is the start of the line and staying is how one moves up (social queuing: Kokko and Johnstone 1999); play the decrement weak for a junior who expects to rise.

pre_language.increment: High in the order, she takes first pick and others give way, and she goes after what she wants confident of getting it.
pre_language.decrement: Low in the order, she waits on others' leavings, and expects to miss out on what she wants.

reactive_test.reason: A felt forecast drawn from emotionally weighted evidence of where shares reach her; the pre-language forms are confident pursuit and resigned waiting.

forces.name: Repaid in order of rank
forces.increment_logic: Going first as a matter of course, I find that what I give comes back promptly and in full: those below answer my favours with service before anyone else's, and my sense that my partners pay me back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: Going last as a matter of course, I find that the service I pass up comes back late and short: cover and favour from above reach me only after everyone above me has been served, and my sense that my partners pay me back falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked primate groups grooming runs up the order: low-ranked animals groom high-ranked ones more than they are groomed in return (Seyfarth 1977; Schino 2001), and what comes back to them is mostly tolerance and occasional support, with grooming exchanged in part for agonistic support (Schino 2007). Under this deck's face that tolerance and support count as a return across rank; precedence orders how soon and how fully it comes, as it orders shares, so the same exchange reads as well repaid from the top and thinly repaid from the bottom. The card moves her felt reading of returns from partners, not her readiness to help, and not whether others do their part of the shared work (Dependability).

forces.name: Faltering venture tightens ranks
forces.increment_logic: When I feel those at the top cannot steer us through what we have taken on, our settled ways look like all that still holds us on course, so a member doing things differently or pressing to change our ways jars me as wrong and I am quick to pull them up: my indignation at breaches rises.

forces.explanation: Deck H; the source is Team Confidence's hierarchical face. A felt threat to the venture narrows attention onto the established way of doing things and makes departures feel dangerous, while a venture in safe hands leaves slack for them. The nearest small-group evidence: in freely interacting groups an opinion deviate was rejected more when the dissent came close to the group's decision deadline, which the authors put down to a heightened need for collective closure (Kruglanski and Webster 1991). That study manipulated time pressure, not doubt about the venture; reading a faltering venture as raising the same need for closure is an inference. Under threat, control constricts (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981; carried over, not rechecked here). The face adds its own step, a proposal: in a ranked group the settled ways are partly the top's standing direction, so when live steering from the top looks weak, members lean harder on those ways and a departure reads as one more push off course; when steering looks sure, the top is trusted to catch a stray move, and it passes. The same holds where she is at the top herself and doubts her own steering. Boundaries. The decrement covers departures that do not cross a call from the top; a member who defies the top's own direction is challenging the order, which moves Rule-Keeping through other cards (H:Rank->Rule-Keeping), so keep the decrement small. Where the settled way is itself the top's failing course and the failure is openly acknowledged, departures read as a needed correction (problemistic search: Cyert and March), and since failure is readily laid at the leaders' door (Meindl, Ehrlich and Dukerich 1985), that reading is close to hand in a ranked group; there the pull to guard the ways and the pull to welcome change offset each other, so the card does not fire and the step is nil. The card covers the acute, felt jar of a venture slipping out of the leaders' grip, and the effect should be modest.

pre_language.decrement: When the prize looks well within the band's reach, she lets a fellow try an odd way of doing it without a second look. Her bristle at breaches subsides.

reactive_test.reason: Narrowed attention and a pull back to familiar routines under threat are unbidden and have animal analogues, but the step from that rigidity to indignation at others' departures is shown mainly at organisational and societal scale, and chimpanzees do not police third-party breaches, so the pre-language analogue is weaker than for the other two cards.

forces.framework: Need for closure and rejection of deviates (Kruglanski and Webster 1991); threat rigidity (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981); romance of leadership (Meindl et al. 1985) as boundary; own proposal for the step through the hierarchical face.

sources.source: Staw, Sandelands and Dutton, 1981, Threat rigidity effects in organizational behavior: a multilevel analysis
sources.claim: Under threat, individuals narrow attention to dominant cues, groups and organisations centralise and restrict information, and decision-makers fall back on learned solutions rather than innovating.

sources.source: Gelfand et al., 2011, Differences between tight and loose cultures: a 33-nation study
sources.claim: Societies with histories of ecological and historical threat have stronger norms and less tolerance of deviance; a societal-level association, not a test of a member's reaction to her group's venture.

sources.source: Hogg, Sherman, Dierselhuis, Maitner and Moffitt, 2007, Uncertainty, entitativity, and group identification

forces.note: The direction is consistent across the literatures I know, but none of them tests a member's felt indignation at a fellow's breach as a function of her confidence in the group's venture, and one search turned up only an unpublished null result on threat and the black sheep effect. Do not read this card as damping: threat rigidity is described as often dysfunctional, and later work argues it can feed further threat, so the loop through NormExp may deepen a faltering venture rather than rescue it. Threat rigidity also centralises control, which in a hierarchical culture may load onto high-Status members and lower others' Levelling; that is outside this card.

logic_status.common_sense: The step through the hierarchical face: settled ways stand in for weak live steering, and sure steering leaves slack. This is marked as a proposal and is safe as plain sense. The defiance boundary is also common sense. So is the offset boundary, where an openly failing course makes departures read as a correction.

forces.name: Shirkers sharpen the bristle
forces.increment_logic: When I keep having to check up on, chase and redo what others took on, the next member who departs from the way we do the shared work jars me at once as plainly wrong, as if it were one more corner cut, and I pull them up with a sharp word or a turned back: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I can leave any part of the work with any member, a member doing the shared work their own way strikes me as harmless, coming from people who deliver, and I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
forces.explanation: Anger at free riders drives costly punishment of them (Fehr and Gächter 2002). The evidence concerns breaches of the cooperative task rather than any departure from the group's ways, so the card is limited to the way the shared work is done: where shirking is rife, a different way of doing the work is read as another dodge. On the decrement side, conditional cooperators keep giving when others are seen to contribute (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001); the step from there to letting a departure pass among people who deliver is a proposal resting on common sense. Idiosyncrasy credit, used here before as the brake, is dropped as support: direct tests are few, the leniency it implies is conditional, and the black sheep effect cuts across it. Keep the decrement smaller than the increment.

pre_language.increment: When the others keep leaving their end of the carry or the watch to her, she bristles sooner at any of them doing a thing the wrong way and moves to pull them up: a protest cry, a shove, a cold shoulder. Her norm guarding rises.
pre_language.decrement: When the others reliably hold their end of the shared task, she meets a fellow's odd way of doing things with a shrug and goes about her business. Her bristle at breaches subsides.

reactive_test.reason: Anger at those who leave her the work is an unbidden emotional reaction with a clear primate analogue in retaliation for one's own losses; the generalisation to third-party breaches is human-specific but already present in toddlers' protest, and the card moves felt indignation, not a planned sanctioning strategy. It bears on Engagement through NormExp.

sources.source: Fehr and Gächter, 2002, Altruistic punishment in humans
sources.claim: Punishment expenditure rises with how far a member's contribution falls below the others'; negative emotions toward defectors appear to be the proximate mechanism.

sources.source: Fehr and Fischbacher, 2004, Third-party punishment and social norms
sources.claim: Up to about 60% of unaffected observers punish violations of a cooperation norm, at a cost to themselves; second parties punish more strongly than third parties.

sources.source: Hollander, 1958, Conformity, status, and idiosyncrasy credit
sources.claim: Members who have met the group's expectations earn latitude to depart from its norms without censure; failing to perform an expected task spends that credit. Supports the brake: a reliable crew's departures are tolerated.

sources.source: Kerr, Rumble, Park, Ouwerkerk, Parks, Gallucci and van Lange, 2009, How many bad apples does it take to spoil the whole barrel?
sources.claim: The threat of exclusion counters a few bad apples but not a majority of them. A boundary: where most shirk, sanctioning gives way to withdrawal.

sources.claim: Negative emotions towards defectors are the proximate mechanism of altruistic punishment of free riders.

sources.claim: Idiosyncrasy credit, earned by positively disposed impressions, permits deviation from group expectancies.

sources.claim: Anger at defectors drives punishment

sources.source: Fischbacher, U., Gächter, S., Fehr, E., 2001, Are people conditionally cooperative?, Economics Letters 71
sources.claim: Contribution tracks others' contribution

sources.source: Idiosyncrasy credit (Hollander) and later tests
sources.claim: Leniency towards deviant leaders is conditional and not specified by the theory

forces.note: The evidence is strongest where shirkers are a minority. Where most members shirk, public-goods groups mostly respond by cutting their own contributions rather than sanctioning, so the rise may level off near the floor of OutResp; a cap or a saturating increment is advisable. Status and Levelling gate the outward sign: a low-ranked or cowed member may feel the bristle but pull up only those at or below her, so intimates may under-read it. This card feeds NormExp but I found no defensible return path from NormExp to OutResp (see X:NormExp->OutResp), so it does not by itself close a balancing loop.

timing.why: The OutResp level she brings to the moment colours how she reads a different way of working. She reads it on sight as one more corner cut, and the sharp word or turned back comes straight away.

era.why: OutResp's reading of reliability is older, but the NormExp end is third-party indignation at departures from the group's settled ways of working, which rests on shared norms. One Homo sapiens end makes the card Homo sapiens.

forces.subtitle: Shirking makes odd methods feel wrong
forces.summary: When a member keeps having to check up on, chase and redo what others took on, the next member who departs from the way the shared work is done jars her at once as another corner cut. When she can leave any part of the work with anyone, a different way of working looks harmless and she lets it pass. Dependability and Rule-Keeping move in opposite directions.

problems.where: explanation: 'Anger at free riders drives costly punishment of them (Fehr and Gächter 2002).'
problems.detail: All four checks of Fehr and Gächter 2002 on this item have a null verdict. The same paper checked for X:Reciprocity->NormExp was rated partly, because the emotion evidence is questionnaire-based. 'Drives' overstates that. Fehr and Fischbacher 2004 (supports) is available and uncited.

problems.where: explanation: 'so the card is limited to the way the shared work is done: where shirking is rife, a different way of doing the work is read as another dodge.'
problems.detail: The free-riding evidence concerns contribution shortfalls, not departures in method. Reading a departure in method as a dodge is the card's own step, and the text presents it as a consequence of the evidence.

problems.where: explanation (missing)
problems.detail: There is no boundary for the case where nearly everyone shirks. The sibling card X:Reciprocity->NormExp makes its increment weak or nil there. Kerr et al. 2009 (partly) shows that exclusion threats fail against a majority of bad apples.

problems.where: explanation: 'and the black sheep effect cuts across it'
problems.detail: Not in the literature and not checked. The other two reasons for dropping idiosyncrasy credit are enough.

logic_status.common_sense: Where she has been left to chase and redo others' work, she reads a different way of doing the shared work as another dodge; among people who deliver, she lets the same departure pass. This is safe as plain sense if it is marked as the card's step and kept to the way the shared work is done. A weak increment where nearly everyone shirks is also common sense, matching the sibling card X:Reciprocity->Rule-Keeping.

forces.name: Hoarders stir the levellers
forces.increment_logic: When what I give the group stops coming back and what I need goes unmet, though sharing is still our way, a member stepping outside our settled ways of sharing and helping strikes me as wrong at once, and I am quick to mock or cold-shoulder them: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When whoever has gives to whoever needs and what I put in comes back from any member, a member who is slow to share or helps in a way of his own strikes me as no great matter, since it all comes back in the end, and I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
forces.explanation: When help stops coming back, a member's patience with those who step outside the ways of sharing and helping runs out. About half of people cooperate conditionally: they give as long as others give and withdraw as others free ride (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001). Anger at free riders drives costly punishment of them, even among strangers (Fehr and Gächter 2002). The increment rests on her own giving going unreturned. She is the cooperator who has been left short, and from that position the next departure from the ways of sharing jars at once. Anger and punishment there grow with how far a defector falls below what the others give (Fehr and Gächter 2002). Where nobody shares any more, holding back is therefore no departure from what the group actually does, and the increment is weak or nil; it holds while she still reads sharing as the group's settled way. On the decrement side, a member secure in the return can afford to overlook an occasional lapse, as generous partners do when exchange is noisy (Van Lange, Ouwerkerk and Tazelaar 2002). For the same reason, a flat refusal to share may still stand out the more in a high-giving group, so the decrement eases her reaction to small departures only; keep it smaller than the increment. The evidence concerns the sharing norm, so the card covers only the ways of sharing and helping; breaches in how the shared work is done belong to X:Dependability->Rule-Keeping. The card reads her guarding of a settled way of sharing, which is Rule-Keeping's face; the levelling of a grabber who takes more than his due and makes it stick is Parity's ground and stays there, as Parity's definition draws it. The felt jar may run ahead of the voiced rebuke where her Rank or Parity is low.

pre_language.increment: When her food goes out and nothing comes back while others hide their surplus, she bristles at fellows doing things the wrong way and moves to demand, protest or turn her back; her norm guarding rises.
pre_language.decrement: When food passes freely and comes back to her from whoever next has, a fellow's odd way of doing things draws no bristle; her norm guarding falls.

reactive_test.reason: Demand sharing, protest at the stingy and coalitional mockery of the self-aggrandising have pre-language and forager analogues; the response is indignant rather than calculated; it acts on Engagement through NormExp.

forces.framework: Conditional cooperation (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001); altruistic punishment (Fehr and Gächter 2002).

sources.source: Peterson, 1993, Demand sharing: reciprocity and the pressure for generosity among foragers, American Anthropologist 95: 860-874
sources.claim: Forager sharing runs largely on demands and pressure for generosity, not unsolicited giving: the egalitarian return is enforced.

sources.source: Wiessner, 2005, Norm enforcement among the Ju/'hoansi Bushmen: a case of strong reciprocity?, Human Nature 16: 115-145
sources.claim: Breaches, including stinginess, are met mainly with criticism and mockery; enforcement is common though its effect on behaviour is limited.

sources.source: Boehm, 1993, Egalitarian behavior and reverse dominance hierarchy, Current Anthropology 34: 227-254
sources.claim: Egalitarian bands keep would-be dominants and hoarders in check by ridicule, criticism and ostracism.

sources.source: Fischbacher, U., Gächter, S., Fehr, E., 2001, Are people conditionally cooperative?, Economics Letters 71
sources.claim: Half of subjects are conditional cooperators

sources.source: Fehr, E., Gächter, S., 2002, Altruistic punishment in humans, Nature 415
sources.claim: Negative emotion towards defectors drives punishment

forces.note: The ethnography shows that sharing norms are policed, not that a member's standing reading of poor return raises her general indignation; that step is my inference. At the floor (Reciprocity 1-2) withdrawal and exit may replace indignation, so the push should taper there. Overlaps OutResp->NormExp; if both fire on one event, cap the combined move.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment's source state ('those with a surplus hide it') describes keeping more than one's due, which is Levelling's ground, when it should be the failed return on help. Both lines spread the indignation to any departure from 'our settled ways of sharing and doing', but the literature cited (demand sharing, pressure on hoarders) supports only the sharing norm. Limiting the card to sharing and help also stops it from duplicating X:OutResp->NormExp, which covers the shared work.

Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 1.47 pm (organisational psychologist's critique and Reputation pack questions): The old grounding (forager pressure on the stingy) is the egalitarian levelling form that NormExp's own pre-language assigns to Levelling, so the card contradicted its target. Conditional cooperation supports the same lines without the contradiction.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass. In the explanation, the grabber boundary is put down to NormExp's pre-language, but the current NormExp text says nothing about grabbers. Levelling's definition is the one that draws it (taking more than one's due and making it stick). One sentence opens with 'This is', against the house style. The card name ('levellers') points into Levelling's ground, and the explanation already proposes a new name.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement line has a member who feels help comes back left unmoved by any departure from the ways of sharing. The explanation's support, that there is 'little to bristle at' when sharing flows, concerns how often breaches occur. NormExp reads how strongly a breach strikes her. In public goods games a defector in a high-contributing group deviates further from the others and draws more punishment (Fehr and Gächter 2002), so a flat refusal to share may jar more when it is rare. Secure return does support overlooking small or occasional lapses, as generous partners do under noise. The line should be limited to that, and the decrement kept smaller than the increment, as on the sister card X:OutResp->NormExp. The name 'Hoarders stir the levellers' still points at Levelling's ground; the rename the explanation already proposes should be adopted. New citation (Van Lange, Ouwerkerk and Tazelaar 2002) to be logged in docs/literature.md as unchecked.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The explanation ends with an editing note ('Rename: ...') that does not belong in card text. The card name itself, 'Hoarders stir the levellers', points to Levelling's ground, and the explanation sets that ground aside. The name field cannot be changed through this schema, so the rename to 'Short-changed, short-tempered' is flagged here for Ben. The lines, type and literature pass.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines, the type and the boundaries pass: the source anchors are Reciprocity's egalitarian face and the target signs (mockery, cold shoulder, letting it pass) are NormExp's. The explanation has a gap in its literature. Conditional cooperation predicts that she withdraws her own giving when others do not give; it does not predict indignation. In Fehr and Gächter (2002), anger and punishment grow with how far a defector falls below what the others give. So in a group where nobody shares any more, a hoarder is no departure and the increment should be weak. As written, the explanation uses that deviation logic for the decrement caveat but not for the increment, which is inconsistent. The fix grounds the increment in her own unreturned giving and adds the limiting case. The name 'Hoarders stir the levellers' points to Levelling's ground, which the explanation itself excludes. A name change is outside the JSON fields and is suggested for Ben (for example 'Hoarders jar the sharers').

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Explanation overstates the source: Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr (2001) classed about half their participants as conditional cooperators, with about a third free riders, so 'Most people' should read 'About half of people'. Lines, type and boundaries pass.

Ripple round 6, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment line states the source at its floor ('seems to go into a hole', the Reciprocity 1 anchor, where those with a surplus hide it and sharing is no longer the group's way), yet the explanation says the increment is weak or nil there and holds only while she still reads sharing as the settled way. The line contradicts the card's own scope; the smallest fix is to state the source as low but with sharing still the norm. Separately, the name 'Hoarders stir the levellers' points at Levelling, which the explanation expressly keeps off this card; the name is outside the JSON fields, so this is flagged for Ben.

Ripple round 10, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and explanation pass. Only the name fails: 'stir the levellers' points to Levelling, although the explanation keeps the card off Levelling's ground and says it reads NormExp's guarding of a settled way of sharing. Smallest fix is a rename (needs Ben's approval as a card text change), for example 'Left short, quick to bristle'. The fields below are unchanged.

timing.typical: 1 to 3 seconds after the departure from the ways of sharing
timing.why: The card says the departure strikes her as wrong at once. Anger at free riders is a fast felt reaction (Fehr and Gaechter 2002).

era.why: The card is limited to guarding a settled way of sharing and helping, which is NormExp's norm face. Levelling a grabber may be older (Levelling's ground), but third-party enforcement of a sharing norm is human (Riedl et al. 2012).

forces.subtitle: Unreturned sharing sharpens anger at rule-breakers

When what she puts in comes back, she lets small departures pass. Reciprocity and Rule-Keeping move in opposite directions, and the card covers only the ways of sharing and helping.

problems.where: explanation: 'About half of people cooperate conditionally: they give as long as others give and withdraw as others free ride'
problems.detail: The source supports about half of subjects in one strategy-method, one-shot public goods experiment. It does not support half of people in general.

problems.where: explanation: 'Anger at free riders drives costly punishment of them, even among strangers (Fehr and Gächter 2002).'
problems.detail: The checker rated this partly, because the emotion evidence is questionnaire-based. 'Drives' claims more than that.

problems.where: explanation: 'Anger and punishment there grow with how far a defector falls below what the others give (Fehr and Gächter 2002).'
problems.detail: The check on this item covers only the emotion claim. The deviation-dependence of punishment was not covered: on the sibling item its check has a null verdict. The boundary it supports stands on common sense anyway.

problems.where: explanation: '(Van Lange, Ouwerkerk and Tazelaar 2002)'
problems.detail: Not in the literature and not checked. The decrement claim it backs can rest on common sense.

problems.where: explanation: 'The evidence concerns the sharing norm, so the card covers only the ways of sharing and helping'
problems.detail: X:OutResp->NormExp says the same two studies (Fischbacher et al. 2001; Fehr and Gächter 2002) 'concern breaches of the cooperative task'. The same public goods evidence cannot be about the sharing norm on one card and about task breaches on the other. It concerns contributions to a common pool, and each card's reading of it is the model's step.

logic_status.common_sense: Several claims rest on common sense. When nobody shares any more, holding back is no departure, so the increment is weak. A member secure in the return can overlook an occasional lapse. A flat refusal still stands out in a high-giving group. The felt jar may run ahead of the voiced rebuke when her Rank or Parity is low. All of these are safe as plain sense about norms measured against what the group actually does.

forces.name: Low in the order, guarded
forces.increment_logic: When I hold a high place in this group's order, I expect an objection or a slip of mine to be let pass, with no one pouncing on it or turning away, so I let it show without softening it first: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I sit low in the order, I expect any objection or slip of mine to draw a put-down, so I soften every objection, swallow my first reaction and keep my slips out of sight: my felt safety to show myself falls.

forces.name: Heard from where I sit
forces.increment_logic: When I go first as a matter of course, the others take what I put forward to be good before it has shown its worth: they take up my suggestion, bring me the next problem and credit me with the result, and I feel them turn to me for what I bring: my sense that they defer to me for it rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I go last as a matter of course, what I put forward is passed over or credited to someone higher, however good it is, and I watch the next problem go to someone else: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: Rank sets performance expectations, and expectations steer who is listened to and how contributions are judged, in a self-fulfilling way (expectation states theory). Eminent people get more credit for comparable work (Merton). Status hierarchies reinforce themselves through expectations that favour those already ahead (Magee and Galinsky). Her rank colours the others' judgement of what she brings, and their deference follows that judgement, so the reading stays on Esteem's ground; deference owed to the place itself is Rank and is not carried here. The card moves her felt deference through the others' response to what she puts forward. With H:Prestige->Status it forms a reinforcing pair. The brake is Esteem evidence, a visible failure of what she brings. Proposal: the halo should be strongest when the worth of a contribution is hard to judge, since a plain result can be seen whoever offers it.

forces.name: Settling into a place
forces.increment_logic: When the others keep turning to me for what I bring, hand me decisions and leave jobs that matter in my hands, they come to wait for me and give me the first word as a matter of course, and I feel it has become my place: my felt rung in the order rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I bring stops counting and my word is doubted in front of the others, nothing that matters is handed to me, they stop waiting for me and someone else takes the first word, and I give way: my felt rung in the order falls.
forces.explanation: Freely conferred deference is a route to rank (Henrich and Gil-White; Cheng et al.). Contributors are repaid with standing and influence (Willer), and perceived competence buys influence (Anderson and Kilduff). Once established, status holds itself through expectations (Magee and Galinsky). The step from live deference to a place taken for granted is slow. Proposal: each play moves Rank by a small fraction of Esteem's level, so the settling builds over many plays; make the decrement weaker than the increment, because a settled place outlasts the skill that earned it, as seniority and incumbency show every day. This card absorbs the older model's most-used card: being trusted with something that matters is Esteem evidence, and its settling is this card.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)
logic_status.common_sense: Two claims rest on common sense. (1) The step from live deference to a place taken for granted is slow, so each play moves Rank by a small fraction: one show of regard does not make a settled place, and the self-reinforcing persistence of status (Magee and Galinsky, supports) fits a slow build. (2) The decrement is weaker than the increment because a settled place outlasts the skill that earned it: seniority and incumbency are familiar everywhere, and the same self-reinforcement finding points the same way. Neither is contradicted by checked literature. Willer (supports) concerns contribution as the route to status, and Anderson and Kilduff (partly) shows signalled competence winning influence only in short lab tasks; the card claims no more from them than that contribution and perceived competence buy standing and influence, which is within what they show. Henrich and Gil-White and Cheng et al. (both supports) carry the core link from freely conferred deference to rank.

forces.name: Backed into my place
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them and a place is made for me as a matter of course, a turn or a share of mine that someone questions is let stand by the room, the questioner gives way, and I take it without a word: my felt rung in the order rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge and my turn or my share is questioned in front of the others, no one speaks for me, I give way, and others step ahead of me at turns and shares: my felt rung in the order falls.
forces.explanation: In macaques, kin and allied support is central to acquiring rank (Chapais 1992), and grooming is traded for agonistic support (Schino 2007), with grooming directed up the hierarchy for rank-related benefits (Seyfarth 1977; Schino and Aureli 2008). Those findings concern support from particular partners in return for service. That is the ground of H Reciprocity, where a patron covers you. This card reads the acceptance of the group as a whole and takes from the primate work only that a place in the order is held partly by who would let it stand. The human step is a proposal, common sense in any committee: a member kept at the edge whose turn is questioned finds no one speaking for her and gives way, while one kept among them has her turn let stand. Hierarchical acceptance is held at any rung, high or low. The increment therefore only firms up a turn or share that was in doubt and never lifts her above her place; keep it smaller than the decrement. This carries the second half of the older model's most-used card. It is distinct from Esteem: the room's assent is for who she is to them, not for what she brings.

timing.typical: 2 to 10 seconds
timing.why: The challenge to her turn is met or left unmet on the spot, and she yields or holds her place as the allies move to her side or stay silent.

era.why: Coalitionary support for rank, traded for grooming, is well shown in macaques (Chapais; Schino), so the backing and the yielding have direct primate analogues.

forces.subtitle: Being included props up your place

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "kin and allied support is central to acquiring rank (Chapais 1992)"
problems.detail: The checker could not identify a Chapais 1992 paper, and the cited URL points to Chapais, Girard and Primi 1991 on non-kin alliances, which does not state the claim. The paper that does support it is Chapais and Larose 1988 (supports, abstract). The citation needs to name that paper.

problems.where: explanation: "takes from the primate work only that a place in the order is held partly by who would let it stand"
problems.detail: The same Chapais and Larose 1988 abstract reports that among peers, keeping rank need not depend on kin support when subordinates cannot form coalitions, and Chapais and St-Pierre 1997 is reported (from its title) as finding kin bonds unnecessary for keeping matrilineal rank. The primate work supports support as a route to winning rank, which fits a challenge to a turn or share, and does not support rank being held by support. The word 'held' overreaches.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "with grooming directed up the hierarchy for rank-related benefits (Seyfarth 1977; Schino and Aureli 2008)"
problems.detail: Schino and Aureli 2008 rated partly: its finding is grooming exchanged for grooming, and rank-related benefits appear only as cited background. Seyfarth 1977 alone carries the upward-grooming claim, and it is a model whose tests are mixed.

logic_status.common_sense: The human step is offered as common sense: a member kept at the edge whose turn is challenged finds no one speaking for her and gives way, while one kept among them has the challenge fail. That is safe as ordinary experience of groups and committees, and it is labelled as a proposal. The rule that the increment only firms up a turn or share already in doubt, and stays smaller than the decrement, also rests on common sense: acceptance can be held at any rung, so it defends a place rather than raising one.

forces.name: Friends get the rope
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I hand them parts of the shared work without a second thought, and the times they carried work through come to mind before the lapses: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am left at the edge, I keep the work in my own hands, check what little I hand over, and the last let-down comes back to me as the verdict on them: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: Chimpanzees extend trust to friends more than to non-friends in a non-verbal trust game, though friends are no more trustworthy once trusted (Engelmann and Herrmann 2016). Trust games read whether what is entrusted comes back, which lies near Reciprocity; carrying the finding to confidence that members do their part of the work is by analogy. The felt shift at the cue is in how readily she trusts; the gain for Dependability builds across plays from sampling: a member who trusts more sees more work carried through, while one who withholds trust sees little and keeps her last let-down as the verdict, since withheld trust gets no feedback that could correct it (Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010; Denrell 2005). Control read as distrust lowers the other's effort (Falk and Kosfeld 2006), an effect that is real but usually small on replication (Ziegelmeyer, Schmelz and Ploner 2012), so over many plays withheld trust is partly self-fulfilling. Elaboration: when the low reading comes from being shut out, her reaction may show hostility, aimed readily at whoever crosses her next, even someone who had no part in it, and withheld only from those who treat her warmly (Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001).

sources.source: Engelmann, J., Herrmann, E., 2016, Chimpanzees trust their friends, Current Biology 26: 252-256
sources.claim: Chimpanzees chose to trust friends significantly more than non-friends; friends and non-friends were equally trustworthy.

sources.source: Falk, A., Kosfeld, M., 2006, The hidden costs of control, American Economic Review 96: 1611-1630
sources.claim: Most agents reduce performance when controlled and say they read control as distrust.

sources.source: Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke, 2001, If you can't join them, beat them: effects of social exclusion on aggressive behavior, JPSP 81
sources.claim: Social exclusion raises aggression towards those who rejected the person and towards neutral others.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and mechanism pass. The increment matches high Belonging (drawn in) and OutResp rising (leaving work in their hands); the decrement matches low Belonging (left at the edge) and OutResp falling (checking up), and neither line uses the others' trust in her, skill or the return on help. The sampling account matches Fetchenhauer and Dunning (2010) and Denrell (2005), and control lowering effort matches Falk and Kosfeld (2006). No other card links Belonging to OutResp. The elaboration repeats the Twenge et al. (2001) misstatement found on E:Belonging->Levelling: the aggression they measured fell on an insulter or a neutral stranger, never on the excluders. The fix uses the same correction as that card.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Timescale. Cards act within seconds or minutes of a cue, but both lines narrate a process that takes many plays: handing work over and then seeing it carried through (increment), and checking, the others reading it as distrust and slackening, then a let-down (decrement). The explanation itself grounds the gain in sampling, which is an across-plays effect. The lines should give the felt reaction at the cue and leave the sampling and the Falk and Kosfeld feedback to the explanation as what builds over many plays. Smaller point: 'my friends among them' narrows OutResp, which reads the other members generally. Literature checks out: Engelmann and Herrmann (chimpanzee friends trusted more, not more trustworthy), Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010 and Denrell 2005 (withheld trust gets no corrective feedback), Falk and Kosfeld (hidden costs of control), Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001 (excluded people aggress against a neutral target, not against one who praised them). Boundaries and type are sound.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The explanation's last clause sends a public exclusion 'read as a slight to her good name' to the Reputation expansion. The revised Face moves only on an open charge, or a witnessed instance, of wronging people or shirking one's share, and it excludes being wanted (Belonging). Repute reads the private verdict on her conduct. Being shut out is neither of these, so the clause misroutes the flare. Smallest fix: drop the clause. Also added the missing years for Engelmann and Herrmann (2016) and Falk and Kosfeld (2006), and noted that the control effect is small on replication, in line with E:OutResp->Repute.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines and type pass against both definitions, and the citations hold as stated. The trust games cited (Engelmann and Herrmann 2016; Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010) measure trust that a partner will return what is entrusted, which is close to Reciprocity's ground (the return on what you give), while OutResp reads whether members carry through their part of shared work. The explanation presents them as direct evidence for OutResp without saying the carry-over is by analogy. Only Falk and Kosfeld, a principal-agent effort setting, bears on work directly. Smallest fix: one clause in the explanation saying so.

timing.typical: within the task, as she hands out the next piece of work
timing.why: Warm or cold treatment shifts at once how readily she trusts and which memories come up, and the felt confidence settles as she decides what to hand over; the larger gain builds over many plays.

era.why: Chimpanzees extend more trust to friends in a non-verbal trust game (Engelmann and Herrmann 2016), and leaving a part of joint work to a partner has early human analogues before words are given.

forces.subtitle: Friends are trusted to do their part
forces.summary: Feeling drawn in as one of the group makes a member readier to trust the others with shared work and to remember times they came through. Feeling left at the edge makes her keep the work close, check what she hands over and treat the last let-down as the verdict. Withheld trust gets no correction, so Dependability builds or erodes across plays.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 3: "...since withheld trust gets no feedback that could correct it (Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010; Denrell 2005)."
problems.detail: Neither Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010 nor Denrell 2005 appears among the cited sources, and neither has a checker's verdict. The sentence carries the card's mechanism for the gain to Dependability building across plays, so the card's main mechanism has no checked support.

problems.where: increment_logic: "the times they carried work through come to mind before the lapses"; decrement_logic: "the last let-down comes back to me as the verdict on them"
problems.detail: These are claims about memory at the cue, and no source makes them. The explanation's own account is a slower sampling effect across plays, not a recall bias within seconds, so the lines claim more than the explanation and its sources show. The fix restates them as acts she can observe.

problems.where: explanation, final sentence: "Elaboration: when the low reading comes from being shut out, her reaction may show hostility... (Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001)."
problems.detail: Twenge et al. rated partly: aggression is a behaviour, and the source says nothing about one's assessment of others, which is Dependability's ground. The checker also flags the exclusion-aggression effect as contested. The sentence describes conduct rather than the target reading. Drop it from this card.

logic_status.common_sense: The carry from the chimpanzee trust game to confidence that members do their part of the work is declared as analogy; it is safe as common sense in that people drawn into a group extend more working trust to its members. The sampling argument (withheld trust gets no feedback that could correct it) is sound reasoning on its own, but it is currently attributed to sources nobody has checked; the fix recasts it as common sense pending a check.

forces.name: Generous, so sought
forces.increment_logic: When the partners I help pay me back as a matter of course, I give help freely, beyond any one partner and where the others can see it; they see what I bring, seek me out with their problems and take my advice, and I feel them turn to me: my sense that they defer to me for what I bring rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the partners I help do not pay me back, I stop giving beyond what I must; the others see less given by me and bring me fewer of their problems: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls a little.
forces.explanation: In public settings, the most generous members gain the most status, here freely given deference (Esteem), and are the most preferred partners (Hardy and Van Vugt 2006), and contributors are given influence and deference (Willer 2009). Both studies concern contributions to a common pool; the step to help given beyond her own partners in the others' sight is by analogy. A felt return makes open-handed giving affordable to her, and the deference comes from the giving the others see, not from the return; giving the others read as a paid trade earns less of it. Each play moves her felt reading a step; the deference builds over many plays. Her name as a sharer is Repute's ground and is not carried here. The card carries the older build's Acceptance->Standing, with the giving now driven by felt return. It forms a positive loop with H:Prestige->Reciprocity; the brake is a partner who stops repaying.

sources.source: Hardy, C., Van Vugt, M., 2006, Nice guys finish first: the competitive altruism hypothesis, PSPB 32: 1402-1413
sources.claim: When contributions were public, the most altruistic members gained the highest status and were most preferred as partners.

sources.source: Willer, R., 2009, American Sociological Review 74
sources.claim: Contributors receive status, influence and gifts, and those given status contribute more later.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Decrement line: 'what I give is not returned' does not mark the hierarchical face, which reads the return from the partner helped, as the increment line does. 'No one now knows me as one who gives' overstates a felt reaction of minutes: a reputation for giving does not vanish at once, though the others see her give less. Increment line, type and literature (Hardy and Van Vugt on competitive altruism; Willer on contributors given deference) are fine.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines pass on source, target, type and boundaries, and the mechanism agrees with competitive altruism (Hardy and Van Vugt) and Willer. The explanation fails in two ways. It does not say that the chain (her giving, then others coming to know her as a giver) is a reputation that builds over many plays, although cards act within minutes. It also opens with 'This is my build's', which breaks the prose style and uses an author's first person out of keeping with the other explanations. Smallest fix is to the explanation only.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment runs the rise through 'they come to know me as one who gives', which is her name as a sharer: Repute's ground (sharing what you have), as the Reciprocity definition itself marks. Prestige rises on deference for what she brings, so the line should go from visible giving to being sought and heeded without passing through a verdict on her character. The explanation says the generous gain 'status'; in Model B the deference Hardy and Van Vugt and Willer describe is Prestige, not the settled order (Status), and 'the reputation as a giver builds' carries the same Repute slip. The decrement passes.

Ripple round 11, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Explanation only. It says a felt return makes open-handed giving 'cheap', which sits badly with its own sources: competitive altruism credits giving as a costly display (Hardy and Van Vugt), and observers give less credit to giving they see as repaid or self-interested. The mechanism holds if the return makes giving affordable to her while the deference rests on the giving the others see. The explanation should also mark that giving seen as a paid trade earns less deference. Lines, type and direction pass.

Ripple round 12, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass against hierarchical Reciprocity and Prestige, and keep the sharer's name off the card (Repute). The explanation refers to 'Model B's terms', which is defined nowhere in the model texts, and cites Hardy and Van Vugt (2006) and Willer (2009) without years.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The support (Hardy and Van Vugt 2006; Willer 2009) concerns contributions to a group's common pool, made in public. The increment line has her giving only to the partners she helps, and on the hierarchical face that giving is partner trade, which the explanation itself says earns less deference. Prestige's ground is contribution the group values, so the giving that earns deference has to reach past the one partner. Name the analogy in the explanation. The decrement and type pass.

Ripple round 6, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement overstates. Esteem's hierarchical face rests on skill, knowledge and contribution, generosity only one part of it. Cutting back her giving thins only the generosity part, so 'they stop seeking me out, and I feel passed over' claims a loss of the whole deference. The fall should be small and limited to what her giving earned.

logic_status.common_sense: Three claims rest on common sense. (1) A felt return makes open-handed giving affordable to her: help that is repaid costs less, so she can give more widely. (2) Giving the others read as a paid trade earns less deference: observers discount generosity that looks self-serving, an ordinary attribution, and it fits Hardy and Van Vugt's finding that status rewards rose with the cost of the altruism. (3) The decrement falls only a little: when repayment stops she still gives what she must, so some visible giving remains. None is contradicted by checked literature. The core link, that public generosity earns status and partner preference and that contributors receive influence and deference, rests on Hardy and Van Vugt 2006 and Willer 2009 (both supports). The card itself flags the step from common-pool contribution to help beyond her own partners as analogy.

forces.name: Low rung, easy target
forces.increment_logic: When I hold a high place in the order, no one tries to push me about or take my due, and I go about my business beside the strongest without a glance at their mood: my sense that no one here can force me or take more than their due and keep it rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I sit low in the order, the one who likes to push finds me the easy target, taking more of my turns and my share than the order gives him, leaning on me, and passing me over when he hands things out to his own; I start to watch him and do what heads off his temper: my sense that no one here can force me, take more than their due or hand out unfairly, and get away with it, falls.
forces.explanation: Rank shapes how much aggression and stress an animal receives, but direction and size depend on the society: subordination is most stressful in despotic species and not in egalitarian ones (Sapolsky 2005), and formalised, reconciled orders damp overt aggression (de Waal 1986). In a settled order she accepts, a low place moves Parity little, and an even-handed share-out that gives her less by rank leaves it high, as the Parity definition says; the card bites when someone uses her low place to push, take or pass her over. Set it small in settled orders and larger in despotic ones.

problems.where: increment_logic: "When I hold a high place in the order, no one tries to push me about or take my due..." and explanation: "Set it small in settled orders and larger in despotic ones."
problems.detail: Sapolsky 2005, the card's own main source (supports), says which ranks bear more stress depends on whether the hierarchy is stable: in unstable orders the high-ranked face the most challenges. The increment states without condition that a high place brings freedom from being pushed, and the explanation's scaling covers settled and despotic orders but never contested ones, where the increment should vanish.

problems.where: increment_logic, final clause: "my sense that no one here can force me or take more than their due and keep it rises"
problems.detail: The decrement names the target as no one being able to force her, take more than their due or hand out unfairly, and get away with it. The increment leaves out unfair share-outs, so the two lines describe different readings of Parity. The increment should match the decrement's wording and add the share-out face.

logic_status.common_sense: The human step, that a pusher picks the low-ranked as an easy target and that a high place shields one from being pushed in a settled order, rests on common sense about bullying and is safe as stated for settled orders. The primate sources (Sapolsky, supports; de Waal, partly, read as formalised orders damping overt aggression) back only the moderating role of the society.

forces.name: Ideas aired, ideas taken up
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a half-formed idea show, I put forward how we might do the work better in front of the others; they take it up and turn to me on it: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and keep my ideas masked, what I could bring stays in my head; the others never see it and turn to whoever spoke up instead: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: Felt psychological safety is the main spur to speaking up in work teams (Edmondson 1999; Detert and Burris 2007). Speaking up raises the status colleagues confer, partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic and competent (Weiss and Morrison 2019). Promotive voice, ideas for doing things better, raised peer-rated status and later leader emergence, while prohibitive voice, raising concerns, did not; men gained from promotive voice and women did not (McClean et al. 2018). Members who act confidently are judged competent and gain influence even when their answers are no better (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). The card covers ideas offered to improve the shared work; voicing alarm or criticism is not covered and may cost her. Where the group's norms follow McClean's pattern, set it smaller for women members; the gap rests on one set of field studies, so treat it as a caution. Deck E: the card reads Esteem's egalitarian face, deference freely given on the matter in hand with no right to command. It forms a Reinforce loop with E:Prestige->DivsExp; the brake is a visible failure of what she puts forward (Esteem evidence).

critique_was.name: Ideas aired, ideas taken up
critique_was.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a half-formed idea show, I put forward how we might do the work better in front of the others; they take it up and turn to me on it: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises.
critique_was.decrement_logic: When I brace and keep my ideas masked, what I could bring stays in my head; the others never see it and turn to whoever spoke up instead: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
critique_was.explanation: Felt psychological safety is the main spur to speaking up in work teams (Edmondson 1999; Detert and Burris 2007). Speaking up raises the status colleagues confer, partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic and competent (Weiss and Morrison 2019). Promotive voice, ideas for doing things better, raised peer-rated status and later leader emergence, while prohibitive voice, raising concerns, did not; men gained from promotive voice and women did not (McClean et al. 2018). Members who act confidently are judged competent and gain influence even when their answers are no better (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). The card covers ideas offered to improve the shared work; voicing alarm or criticism is not covered and may cost her. Where the group's norms follow McClean's pattern, set it smaller for women members; the gap rests on one set of field studies, so treat it as a caution. forces.explanation: In public goods games free riders draw an equal share of the pool while keeping their own stake, so they end ahead of those who contributed, and contributors' anger at them drives costly punishment (Fehr and Gächter 2002). The anger is Rule-Keeping's ground (X:OutResp->NormExp); the card takes from the study only that members read a coaster as ending ahead of what his part earns. Members also cut their own effort rather than carry a capable partner who free rides (the sucker effect: Kerr 1983), which does not move here. A coaster who draws the full share where the group's reckoning ties shares to doing one's part takes more than that reckoning gives, which is what Parity's second limb reads; the reading falls only when no one stops him and the grab sticks. The card holds only under such a reckoning. The game's own rule splits the pool equally, so players' tie of shares to contribution is inferred from the contributors' anger, not given by the game. Where the group's reckoning gives equal shares whatever each puts in, as Ache bands share game whoever made the kill (Kaplan and Hill 1985), the coaster gets what the reckoning gives and Parity is untouched; where reward tracks each member's own output, shirking costs only the shirker. High reliability removes coasting as one route to an unearned share; it says nothing of grabbing or coercion by other means. Modest; forms a Reinforce loop with E:Levelling->OutResp.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Levelling's second limb reads taking more than the group's own reckoning gives and making it stick. A coaster who draws an equal share takes more than his due only where the reckoning ties shares to doing one's part; where the group shares its take equally regardless of input, as many forager bands do (tolerated scrounging), he takes exactly what the reckoning gives. The increment assumes an equity reckoning ('each share matches what each has put in') and the decrement omits 'makes it stick'. 'I feel a sucker for carrying them' strays into Reciprocity (her help unreturned) and into her own effort cut (Kerr's sucker effect proper), and indignation at the shirk is already carried by X:OutResp->NormExp. The explanation's scope clause names the wrong boundary.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and scope pass. Two citations are glossed loosely. Kerr 1983 found that members cut their own effort rather than be the sucker carrying a capable free rider, and it does not report resentment as such. Blurton Jones 1984 calls the mechanism 'tolerated theft' (later writers say 'tolerated scrounging'). Fix: gloss both as the sources state them.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Both lines pass: the source is read at the stated level, the target moves through Levelling's second limb (taking more than the reckoning gives and making it stick), the lines keep off OutResp's work ground and NormExp's indignation, the type fits, and the card does not duplicate its loop partner E:Levelling->OutResp or X:OutResp->NormExp. Two faults in the explanation. (a) It says the reading 'falls further when no one stops him', which implies it falls even when the coaster is stopped; by Levelling's definition a grab only lowers it once it sticks, as the decrement line rightly says. (b) Tolerated theft (Blurton Jones 1984) explains sharing as a holder yielding what costs too much to defend. It does not show a band reckoning that gives equal shares regardless of input, so it is a poor cite for the boundary case; widespread Ache meat sharing irrespective of who made the kill (Kaplan and Hill 1985) fits the point directly. Fehr and Gächter 2002 and Kerr 1983 are cited correctly.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Increment line overreaches: high OutResp (members carry through and keep their word) does not show that 'no one keeps what our reckoning would not give them'; a reliable member can still grab or coerce. High OutResp only removes coasting as a route to an unearned share, so the line should say that. Decrement passes (1)-(4) and keeps to Levelling's second limb, leaving shirking itself to OutResp and indignation to NormExp. Explanation conflict: Fehr and Gaechter 2002 is a public goods game, where the pool is shared equally whatever each puts in, the very setting the card says leaves Levelling untouched. The free rider there ends ahead by keeping his own stake, and the anger itself is NormExp's ground; the explanation should say so and say what separates it from the Ache case. Kerr 1983 (sucker effect) is sound but concerns her own effort, which the card already sets aside. No duplication with other cards.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and boundaries pass against the revised Levelling (second limb: taking more than the group's reckoning gives and making it stick) and the revised OutResp. The explanation overstates its evidence: in a public goods game the formal rule splits the pool equally whatever each puts in, the same structure the card later uses (Ache sharing) to say Levelling is untouched. Players' sense that shares should track contribution is inferred from contributors' anger and punishment, so 'plainly bring with them' overclaims and sits awkwardly beside the Ache case. Smallest fix: state it as an inference from the anger and note the formal equal split. Also spell Gächter as in X:OutResp->NormExp.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment overreaches. High OutResp removes only coasting as a route to an unearned share, and the explanation says it tells her nothing of grabbing or coercion by other means. The line still ends with her whole sense that no one takes more than their due rising at full strength. Ending it with a small rise keeps the line in step with the explanation and with the card's 'Modest' setting.

forces.name: Credit to spend
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring and take my advice, I feel a slip of mine would be put down to a bad day rather than held against me, and I let my doubts and disagreements show: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one turns to me for anything I bring, I feel I have nothing to set against a slip, so I keep more of my doubts and disagreements masked: my felt safety to show myself falls a little.
forces.explanation: Higher professional status goes with greater felt psychological safety (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006), and power releases approach and expression, while low power primes attention to threat and inhibition (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003). Both bear on settled place and power, which X:Status->DivsExp carries. The step to live deference is a proposal resting on common sense: a member the others turn to has something to set against a slip. Hollander's idiosyncrasy credit says members who have earned standing are allowed more latitude, but direct tests are few and weak, so it is not relied on. Deference that fades with what she brings is a thinner cushion than a settled place, so this card should be the weaker of the two.

When no one turns to the member, there is nothing to set against a slip, so more stays masked and Safety falls a little. This is the weaker route from standing to Safety.

critique_was.name: Credit to spend
critique_was.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring and take my advice, I feel a slip of mine would be put down to a bad day rather than held against me, and I let my doubts and disagreements show: my felt safety to show myself rises.
critique_was.decrement_logic: When no one turns to me any more, I feel every slip would be counted against me with nothing to set against it, so I keep my doubts and disagreements masked: my felt safety to show myself falls.
critique_was.explanation: Higher professional status goes with greater felt psychological safety (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006), and power releases approach and expression, while low power primes attention to threat and inhibition (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003). Both bear on settled place and power, which X:Rank->Safety carries. The step to live deference is a proposal resting on common sense: a member the others turn to has something to set against a slip. Hollander's idiosyncrasy credit says members who have earned standing are allowed more latitude, but direct tests are few and weak, so it is not relied on. Deference that fades with what she brings is a thinner cushion than a settled place, so this card should be the weaker of the two.

timing.typical: a few seconds, as a slip or doubt is about to show
timing.why: The sense of having credit to spend, or of having none, bears on the split-second choice to let a doubt show or mask it.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)
logic_status.common_sense: The step from live deference to felt safety: a member the others turn to has something to set against a slip, so a slip is more likely to be put down to a bad day. Safe because the explanation labels it a proposal, declines to rest on idiosyncrasy credit, keeps the literature on settled status and power with X:Status->DivsExp, and sets this card weaker than that one. The decrement is played as 'falls a little', within what common sense carries.

forces.name: Good season, open hands
forces.increment_logic: When the venture looks well within our reach, I am buoyed, I help whoever asks without counting, and the others do the same around me: my reading that help here comes back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the venture looks beyond us, everyone hunches over their own part, help asked for is slow to come and mine goes unreturned: my reading that help here comes back falls.
forces.explanation: Good mood raises helping (Carlson, Charlin and Miller 1988). Mood spreads through a group by contagion, and positive contagion brings more cooperation and less conflict, negative contagion the reverse (Barsade 2002). Confidence in the venture carries that mood, so help flows more freely in a group that expects to win. Under threat, attention narrows and control tightens (Staw et al. 1981); the step to each member guarding her own part belongs to the proposal, since the same work finds groups under threat drawing closer, which is the rally case below. The step from the group's mood to her felt return is a proposal too: common sense, since a side that expects to win is a generous one. Where doubt about the venture rallies the group around a common threat (E:Team Confidence->Belonging), help may keep flowing; play the decrement weak or not at all then. Modest; forms a loop with E:Reciprocity->Team Confidence.

sources.source: Carlson, Charlin and Miller 1988, JPSP 55
sources.claim: Review of 61 positive-mood conditions supports good mood increasing helping

sources.source: Barsade 2002, ASQ 47
sources.claim: Positive emotional contagion improved cooperation and lowered conflict; negative did the opposite

forces.name: Backs to each other
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I see us talk the work through, pass on what we know and pull the same way, and the venture looks within the reach of a side like ours: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am left at the edge, I see the work run in knots that do not talk it through or pass things on, and what I could bring left out of it, and the venture looks beyond the group as it stands: my confidence that the group can pull it off falls.
forces.explanation: Cohesion is related to group performance, and all three of its components count, most for behaviour and efficiency and where work flows intensively between members (Beal et al. 2003). In sport teams, task cohesion early in a season predicts collective efficacy later, as well as the reverse (Heuzé, Raimbault and Fontayne 2006, to be checked). Belonging sits nearest the social component, interpersonal attraction, and the link runs mainly through commitment to the task (Mullen and Copper 1994), so the evidence for this card is indirect. Her Belonging reads the others' acceptance of her, not how close-knit the group is, so the step from her own inclusion to the group's cohesion is a proposal: a member left at the edge sees the group as split, and sees what she brings go unused. Where she is shut out by a group that plainly works well together, the decrement is weak or nil. Performance to cohesion is the stronger direction (Mullen and Copper 1994), carried by E:Team Confidence->Belonging, so set this card smaller than that one. It is distinct from E:Reciprocity->Team Confidence (help that comes back) and E:Dependability->Team Confidence (reliability). With E:Belonging->Dependability and E:Team Confidence->Reciprocity, it fills the last empty ordered pairs among the core deck E Pillars.

timing.typical: within the work session, 5 to 30 minutes
timing.why: She must watch the group work, pulling together or splitting into knots, before her confidence in what it can do follows her inclusion.

era.why: Being drawn into or left outside a coordinated band, and judging what that band can manage together, are pre-linguistic; talking the work through is the modern form of an older coordination.

forces.subtitle: Being included builds belief in the group
forces.summary: When the others draw a member in, she sees the group talk the work through, share what it knows and pull together, so the venture looks within reach. When she is left at the edge, she sees tangled work and her own contribution unused, and the venture looks beyond the group. The effect runs weaker than the opposite direction.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: 'In sport teams, task cohesion early in a season predicts collective efficacy later, as well as the reverse (Heuzé, Raimbault and Fontayne 2006, to be checked).'
problems.detail: Checker verdict not found. The secondary summary of the likely source (Heuzé, Bosselut and Thomas 2007) supported only collective efficacy as an antecedent of task cohesion, so the cohesion-to-efficacy direction this card needs is at risk of contradiction. Drop the sentence.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 3: 'and the link runs mainly through commitment to the task (Mullen and Copper 1994)'
problems.detail: The checked part of Mullen and Copper is the direction of the path, not the task-commitment claim, and a later critique calls that claim premature. Beal et al. 2003 (supports), cited in the sentence before, found each cohesion component independently related to performance. The two sentences sit against each other.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from her own inclusion to her reading of the group's cohesion and of what she brings being used. Safe as labelled: she reads the group from where she sits, and the explanation weakens the decrement where she is shut out by a group that plainly works well.

forces.name: Rising tide
forces.increment_logic: When I feel those at the top can steer us through what we have taken on, I see what I came for riding on a venture in safe hands: a well-led side that wins has places, credit and shares to hand down, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel those at the top cannot steer us through what we have taken on, I see what I came for going down with a venture in the wrong hands: a badly led side has little to hand down and no name to lend me, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for falls.
forces.explanation: Deck H; the source is Team Confidence's hierarchical face. The mechanism is kept: where members' outcomes ride on the group's, the venture's prospects are part of each member's own. Reward interdependence acts on members' effort (Wageman 1995), and loafing falls when members value the group outcome and expect their effort to matter to it (Karau and Williams 1993); both carried over, not rechecked here. In a ranked group those prospects are read through the top: under authority ranking those above direct the joint undertaking and those below look to them for guidance and protection (Fiske 1992), and people credit and blame leaders for group outcomes beyond their share, most for extreme outcomes (Meindl, Ehrlich and Dukerich 1985). Leadership is a working predictor, not only a romance: a team's trust in its coach both followed from and predicted its later performance (Dirks 2000), and in army units the leadership climate at the higher level was the strongest predictor of collective efficacy (Chen and Bliese 2002). Trust in leaders also goes with commitment and lower intent to quit (Dirks and Ferrin 2002), but those trust measures mix competence with good faith, and how fairly the top will share out what the venture yields is Parity's or Reciprocity's ground, not this card's; the card reads only how much a well- or badly-led venture will have to hand out, so take that meta-analysis as light support. No study here measures a member's forecast of her own yield, so the felt step is a proposal resting on common sense: nobody expects to get ahead under leaders who are running the side aground. Where she is at the top herself, her confidence in her own steering feeds her forecast through the venture; what her rung itself brings her is H:Rank->Payoff. Set the card small or nil where her aims do not depend on the venture (a member there for the company, or paid by her own output alone). Because leaders are credited with outcomes after the fact, a run of results can inflate or sink the face beyond the leaders' real grip; the brake is Team Confidence evidence on the venture itself.

forces.name: Backers at my shoulder
forces.increment_logic: When the partners I help pay me back and the one above me covers me, a turn or share of mine that someone questions finds my partners moving to my side; the challenger gives way and I take it as of right: my felt rung in the order rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When my partners take and do not return, a challenge to my turn or share finds no one at my side; I give way, and the one who pressed me goes ahead of me next time too: my felt rung in the order falls.
forces.explanation: In primates grooming given is repaid in agonistic support (36 studies, 14 species, small effect: Schino 2007), and allied and kin support decides how macaque females acquire and hold rank (Chapais 1992). H:Belonging->Status hands partner support to Reciprocity but no card carried it; this one does. Support from particular partners, not the whole room's assent (Backed into my place). The effect per exchange is small, so the step is modest, and the increment is smaller than the decrement: backing firms up a contested turn more than it lifts her above her place.

forces.name: Skill shared, drawn in
forces.increment_logic: When the others watch how I do things and bring me their problems, and I share what I know without lording it, they seek my company and keep a place for me wherever they gather: my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one watches or seeks me for anything I bring, I am the one who has to seek them out, and I read the quiet as being wanted less, though they still count me one of their own: my sense that they want me among them falls a little.
forces.explanation: Prestige-based influence comes with being liked, dominance-based influence does not (Cheng et al. 2013); learners seek proximity to the models they learn from (Henrich and Gil-White 2001); better hunters gain allies and mates (Smith 2004). Under the E face, acceptance does not rest on output, so the rise comes from what she shares freely and modestly, which counts as pulling with the group, and not from the skill itself. Only prestige carried modestly draws people; boasting turns it into levelling talk (pack X:Prestige->Repute). The decrement is small and lies in her reading, not in the group's acceptance: people read how far they are wanted from signs of their relational value, so being sought less feels like being wanted less (Leary and Baumeister 2000). A member who brings little but pulls as far as she is able stays one of their own in good standing, and the card must never edge her out on that ground alone.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "Leaders in small-scale societies hold influence by results and reputation, not by office alone (von Rueden et al. 2014; Garfield, von Rueden and Hagen 2019)"
problems.detail: Neither source as checked supports 'by results and reputation'. The von Rueden et al. check (partly) confirms only that leaders exist and influence collective action in an egalitarian society; the abstract ties their influence to strength, kin and exchange partners, with reputation unconfirmed and results never mentioned. The Garfield et al. check (partly, not read) explicitly could not confirm that the group's success raises a leader's standing. The card's whole route (group prospects to the leader's standing) leans on the very link these checks fail to show.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: "Her own doubt about the top's steering, where she is at the top, shows in hesitant calls that others notice."
problems.detail: No source is cited for this mechanism. It holds up as common sense, but the text needs to say it is a proposal so that it does not read as following from the leadership sources.

logic_status.common_sense: That a top member's private doubt about steering the group shows in hesitant calls, that others notice and step into the first turn, and that her felt rung slips as she gives ground.
